lead: Both readings turn on trust. Paul knows that “not all have faith”, but he rests his hope on a stronger fact: “the Lord is faithful”. In the Gospel a father whose daughter has just died and a woman ill for twelve years come to Jesus with nothing left but that same trust, and neither is sent away. In the season of Denha, when Christ is shown to the world, today’s question is how far we will rely on him.

set: The Christians of Thessalonica, a port city of Macedonia, had been unsettled by talk that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2). The letter comes to us under the name of Paul, and many hold it to be his; some scholars think that a disciple wrote it in his name. After the teaching on the end in chapter 2, and before the warning against idleness in 3:6–15, stands this short passage of prayer and confidence.
The great missionary does not speak here as someone who needs nothing. He asks a small and troubled community to pray for him.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul asks for prayer: that the word may spread, and that the missionaries may be rescued.
vv. 3–4: God’s faithfulness, and Paul’s confidence in the community because of it.
v. 5: a short prayer for their hearts.
kw: Literally “may run”. The word of God is pictured as a runner, an image that recalls Psalm 147:15: “his word runs swiftly”. The missionaries may be held back, but the word itself keeps moving.
The Greek sets two related words side by side: not all have pistis, “but the Lord is pistos”. Our faith may fail. His faithfulness is what holds us.

Endurance, literally remaining under a load. The Greek “steadfastness of Christ” can mean the endurance Christ himself showed, or the endurance he gives. The Malayalam POC takes it as what Christ gives. The two belong together.
vv: pray for us, so that the word of the Lord may spread rapidly and be glorified everywhere
Paul asks first for the word and only then for himself (v. 2). The word is glorified when people receive it and live it.
But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
The Greek for “the evil one” can also be read as “evil”, as in the last petition of the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:13). The Catechism explains that petition as referring to a person, Satan (CCC 2851).
May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ.
To “direct” is to make a road straight. Paul prays for two things only: love and endurance. A Christian who has these can bear not knowing the date of the Lord’s coming.
ch: The Catechism notes how the first communities lived this exchange of prayer: Paul gives them a share in his ministry of preaching, and he intercedes for them in turn (CCC 2636). Those who are sent need the prayer of those who stay. When a parish prays for its priests and missionaries, it is doing what the Thessalonians were asked to do.

r.h: Your faith has made you well
set: Matthew 8–9 gathers a series of mighty works after the Sermon on the Mount, showing that the Teacher also acts with authority. Here two stories are woven together, as they are in Mark 5 and Luke 8. Matthew tells them in very few words. He does not give the leader’s name, and in his account the girl has already died when her father comes.

Two details belong to the world of that time. A woman with a continuing flow of blood was ritually unclean under Leviticus 15:25–27, a state which touched her contact with others and with worship; it was not a judgment on her as a sinner. And the flute players belong to the mourning customs of the day: a later Jewish saying (Mishnah, Ketubot 4:4) expects even the poorest man to provide flutes and a mourner at his wife’s burial.
str: vv. 18–19: the father’s request, and Jesus gets up and goes.
vv. 20–22: on the way, the woman and the fringe of the cloak.
vv. 23–24: the mourners, and the word “sleeping”.
vv. 25–26: he takes her by the hand; the report spreads.
kw: The word can mean the edge of a garment or the tassels that the Law asked Israelites to wear as a reminder of the commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). Jesus appears here dressed as a faithful Jew.
The same Greek verb means both to heal and to save, and it comes three times in vv. 21–22. Her body is healed, and something larger has happened as well.
The ordinary verb for rising from bed, and also the verb Matthew uses of Jesus’ own Resurrection (28:6). The girl’s rising points beyond itself.
vv: for she said to herself, “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.”
Her faith is simple and even a little awkward. She wants to stay unseen. Jesus accepts such faith, but he does not leave her hidden.
Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, “Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.”
He calls her “daughter”, in a story that began with another parent’s daughter. A woman who had suffered for twelve years is told she belongs to a family.
“Go away; for the girl is not dead but sleeping.” And they laughed at him.
Jesus is not denying that she died (v. 18). For him death is a sleep from which he can wake anyone. Compare Daniel 12:2 and what he says of Lazarus in John 11:11.
he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl got up.
He says nothing in Matthew’s account. Touching a corpse made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11), but here the touch runs the other way: life passes from him to her.
ch: The Catechism says that the sick still try to touch Jesus, and that “in the sacraments Christ continues to ‘touch’ us in order to heal us” (CCC 1504). It also teaches that Jesus heard the prayer of faith already in his ministry, through signs that anticipate his death and Resurrection (CCC 2616). St Augustine, preaching on this woman as the other Gospels tell of her, contrasts the crowd that presses around Jesus with the one person who truly touches him: the crowd presses, faith touches (in substance).

qa: Was the girl really dead, if Jesus says she is sleeping?

Her father says she has just died (v. 18), and the mourners are already there. Matthew tells this as a raising from death. “Sleeping” is the biblical way of speaking of death in the light of God’s power. Early Christians would soon call their burial grounds “cemeteries”, from a Greek word for a place of sleep.
study: Paul says, “the Lord is faithful”. When my own faith is weak, what helps me to rest on that?
The woman wanted to touch and remain hidden, and Jesus turned to speak to her. What would I say to him if he turned to me today?

lead: Forty days after his birth the Lord is carried into his Temple, and all four readings meet there. Leviticus gives the law of a mother’s offering, with its concession to the poor, and Luke shows Mary and Joseph keeping that law with the poor person’s gift. Isaiah presents the Servant as “a light to the nations”, and old Simeon, holding the child, says the same words over him. Paul, grieving for his own people, calls Christ the goal to which the law was always moving. The readings fit together around three words: law, light and waiting. The law is kept, the light is seen, and those who waited are at last able to depart in peace.

set: Leviticus 11–15 sets out the laws of ritual purity. These laws do not speak of moral guilt. “Unclean” describes a state that kept a person from the sanctuary for a time. Birth, blood and death stand at the edge of life, where human beings touch the mystery of God who gives life, and the Law surrounds them with care and reverence.

Chapter 12 is short and practical. After bearing a son a mother waits seven days and then thirty-three, forty in all. After bearing a daughter the periods are doubled, eighty in all. The text gives no reason for the difference, and the explanations offered by commentators remain guesses. The boy’s circumcision on the eighth day (v. 3) is mentioned in passing.
str: vv. 1–4: after the birth of a son: seven days, then thirty-three.
v. 5: after the birth of a daughter: two weeks, then sixty-six days.
vv. 6–7: the offering: a lamb and a pigeon or turtledove.
v. 8: the provision for the poor.
kw: A term of worship, not of ethics. The mother has not sinned by giving birth. In the first creation account fruitfulness is God’s own blessing (Genesis 1:28). She is simply kept for a time from contact with what is holy.

The traditional translation, and the Malayalam POC’s too. Many scholars prefer “purification offering” here, since no sin is in question. The offering restores the woman to the worship of the community.
From a verb meaning “to go up”. The whole animal is burned and rises to God as a gift. It speaks of a life given back to the One who gave it.
vv: she shall not touch any holy thing, or come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purification are completed.
The rule looks ahead to a return. The period ends, and the mother comes back to the sanctuary with her offering.

When the days of her purification are completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting a lamb in its first year for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering.
On the feast the Church notices the words “a lamb in its first year”. Mary brings no lamb, and yet she carries one in her arms.

If she cannot afford a sheep, she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering; and the priest shall make atonement on her behalf, and she shall be clean.
The Law makes room for the poor, and the poor woman’s offering is fully valid. Luke quotes this very provision (2:24), and in doing so he tells us quietly how poor the Holy Family was.
ch: The Second Vatican Council notes that Mary presented her Son to the Lord “making the offering of the poor” (Lumen Gentium 57). The Catechism sees the Presentation as showing Jesus to be the firstborn Son who belongs to the Lord (CCC 529), and his circumcision as the sign of his submission to the Law (CCC 527). The purity laws have been fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind Christians (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15). What remains is reverence for the giving of life, and gratitude when a child is born.

set: Chapters 40–55 of Isaiah speak to the Jews in exile in Babylon, promising return. Within them are four passages commonly called the Servant Songs, and this is the first (42:1–4); vv. 5–7 add God’s word addressed to the Servant.

Who is the Servant? Elsewhere in these chapters Israel itself is called God’s servant (41:8; 49:3), and that is how Jewish tradition has generally read it. The Songs also speak of an individual with a mission to Israel (49:5–6). The New Testament sees the Songs fulfilled in Jesus. Matthew quotes this very passage of him (Matthew 12:18–21), and the voice at the baptism echoes its opening line (Matthew 3:17).
str: v. 1: God presents the Servant: chosen, upheld, given the Spirit.
vv. 2–3a: his gentle way: no shouting, no breaking.
vv. 3b–4: his steady persistence until justice is established.
v. 5: the Creator speaks.
vv. 6–7: the Servant’s mission: covenant, light, sight, release.
kw: Not a menial, but one who acts with his master’s authority. Moses and David have the same title. The Servant’s greatness lies in whom he serves.
It comes three times in vv. 1–4. It means more than court verdicts. It is the right order of things that God wills for the world. The Servant’s mission reaches all the nations.

The phrase returns in 49:6. Simeon takes it up in the Temple (Luke 2:32). The title of the Council’s great document on the Church, Lumen Gentium, is the same phrase in Latin, and it opens by saying that this light is Christ.
vv: Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.
“Chosen” and “in whom my soul delights”: at the baptism the Father’s voice says, “with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and the Spirit comes down.
a bruised reed he will not break, and a dimly burning wick he will not quench;

A cracked reed is useless, and a smoking wick is about to go out. Anyone else would throw them away. This Servant does not. Matthew reads these words as a portrait of Jesus’ gentleness toward the weak (Matthew 12:20).
I have given you as a covenant to the people, a light to the nations,
The Servant does not merely bring a covenant and a light. In some way he is the covenant and the light. On this feast the Church hears these words being fulfilled in a child forty days old.
to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness.
In the first place this points to the exiles coming home from Babylon. Jesus’ healing of the blind gives the words a further fullness (Luke 4:18; 7:22).
ch: The Catechism says that the Messiah’s characteristics are revealed above all in the Servant Songs (CCC 713), and that Jesus’ baptism is his acceptance and inauguration of his mission as God’s suffering Servant (CCC 536). The Second Vatican Council begins its constitution on the Church with these words: Christ is the light of the nations, and the Church’s task is to let that light shine on all people (Lumen Gentium 1).

r.h: Christ, the end of the law
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul’s anguished reflection on his own people, the people of the covenant, most of whom had not accepted Jesus as Messiah. He begins by saying that he has “great sorrow and unceasing anguish” in his heart (9:2), and he lists Israel’s gifts with love (9:4–5). These chapters end not in condemnation but in hope and praise: “all Israel will be saved” (11:26), “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).

Today’s passage belongs to the middle of the argument and must be read inside that whole. Paul, himself a Jew, is speaking of a question within his own family. It must never be used to speak against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597, 839).
str: 9:30–31: the surprise: Gentiles have found what they did not seek.
9:32–33: the stumbling stone, from Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16.
10:1–2: Paul’s prayer for his people, and his witness to their zeal.
10:3: God’s righteousness and one’s own.
10:4: Christ is the end of the law.
kw: In Paul, right relationship with God, which God gives and which we receive in faith. It is not first of all a human achievement, though it bears fruit in good deeds.
Paul knows this word from inside: he describes himself as a persecutor “as to zeal” (Philippians 3:6). He speaks of his people’s zeal as a witness and with respect.

The word means both “termination” and “goal”, as when a road reaches the place it was built to reach. The NRSV has “end”, and the Malayalam POC translates it as fulfilment. Many exegetes think Paul’s main sense is the goal: the law was always moving toward Christ.
vv: They have stumbled over the stumbling stone,

In Isaiah the stone is the Lord himself (8:14) and the sure foundation he lays in Zion (28:16). Paul reads it of Christ. The same stone that causes stumbling also saves: “whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (9:33).
Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. I can testify that they have a zeal for God, but it is not enlightened.
Paul’s first response is prayer. He writes as a brother and with no contempt.
For Christ is the end of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
On this feast the verse has a particular force. In the Temple the law is carefully kept (Luke 2:22–24) for the very child toward whom it was moving.
ch: The Catechism says, “Christ is the end of the law” and that only he teaches and bestows the justice of God (CCC 1977). It also teaches that Christ did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it (CCC 577–582). St Augustine, explaining the word “end”, distinguishes between an end that finishes something off and an end that brings it to perfection, and he says that Christ is the second kind (in substance). The Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God never revoked (CCC 121, 839).

r.h: My eyes have seen your salvation
set: Luke’s account of the infancy begins in the Temple with Zechariah (1:8–9) and ends in the Temple with the boy Jesus (2:41–51). This scene stands in the middle. The “law” is mentioned four times in vv. 22–27, and the Holy Spirit three times in vv. 25–27. Luke wants us to see that the old order of the Law and the new breath of the Spirit move together here.

Two laws lie behind v. 22: the mother’s purification (Leviticus 12) and the consecration of the firstborn (Exodus 13:2, 12). Luke does not mention the redemption price of Numbers 18:15–16, and he seems to have in mind the story of Hannah bringing Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:24–28). Behind it all is Malachi’s promise: “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1). He comes in the arms of his mother, and two old people are the only ones who notice.
str: vv. 22–24: the parents keep the law.
vv. 25–28: Simeon, led by the Spirit, takes the child.
vv. 29–32: the canticle of Simeon.
vv. 33–35: the word to Mary: the sign and the sword.
vv. 36–38: Anna the prophet.
kw: The word for what Israel was waiting for, as in Isaiah 40:1: “Comfort, O comfort my people”. Simeon’s whole life is described by what he was looking toward.
A slave’s word for his owner, and the verb for releasing a slave from duty; it is also used of dying. Simeon is a watchman, told at last that he may go off duty.
a sign that will be opposed
Literally “a sign spoken against”. The joy of the canticle is immediately followed by the shadow of the Cross. Jesus will be a sign before which people have to decide.
“The redemption of Jerusalem” (v. 38): the release of a captive or the buying back of what was lost. Anna’s hearers shared Simeon’s hope.
vv: and they offered a sacrifice according to what is stated in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
This is the offering Leviticus 12:8 allows to those who cannot afford a lamb. Luke makes no comment.
Simeon took him in his arms and praised God, saying,
A priest might be expected at this moment, but Luke names no priest, only an old man guided by the Spirit. He holds in his arms the One he has waited for all his life.
Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples,
Simeon is looking at a baby and he calls him salvation. The Church has long prayed this canticle at the close of the day, so that each evening is a small rehearsal for the last one.
a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.

Isaiah’s two horizons meet (42:6; 46:13; 49:6). The Gentiles are named first, but it is Israel’s own glory that shines for them. The salvation of the nations comes through Israel, and it does not replace Israel.
This child is destined for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be opposed

Falling and rising recall Isaiah’s stone (8:14), the same image Paul uses in the third reading. Luke does not say that Israel as a whole falls. “Many” fall and rise, and the words apply to every hearer of the Gospel.
a sword will pierce your own soul too.
The only word in the infancy account spoken directly to Mary about her own pain. The Church reads it in the light of the Cross (CCC 618; Lumen Gentium 58).
She never left the temple but worshiped there with fasting and prayer night and day.

The Greek can mean that she was eighty-four years old, as the NRSV has it, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years. Either way, she stands here as the picture of a long and faithful waiting. A man and a woman together greet the Lord, as so often in Luke.
ch: The Catechism gathers up the scene: with Simeon and Anna all Israel awaits its encounter with the Savior, the name given to this event in the Byzantine tradition; the sword foretold for Mary announces Christ’s perfect and unique offering on the Cross (CCC 529). It also says that it was in the Temple that Joseph and Mary presented him, forty days after his birth (CCC 583). In a homily for this feast St Sophronius of Jerusalem invites all to hasten to meet Christ carrying lights, and to take him up in our arms as Simeon did (in substance). St Ambrose says that whoever wishes to be released in peace must come to the Temple and take the Word of God into the arms of faith (in substance).

qa: Does the Bible teach that childbirth is sinful or that women are unclean?

No. The purity laws deal with worship, not with guilt. Many things that are good and necessary made a person ritually unclean for a time, including burying the dead, which was a work of mercy. The Scriptures treat children as a blessing from the Lord (Psalm 127:3). In the Temple today, a mother and her child are at the centre of God’s saving work.
Did Mary need to be purified?

The Church teaches that Mary was preserved from all sin (CCC 491–493). St Thomas Aquinas taught that the law of purification did not strictly bind her, since her child-bearing was unique, but that she kept it willingly, in humility and obedience, just as her Son was subject to the Law (Summa Theologiae III, q. 37, a. 4; in substance).
Does Romans say that God has rejected the Jewish people?

No. Paul asks that very question and answers: “By no means!” (Romans 11:1). “The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). The Second Vatican Council rests its teaching on these chapters: the Jews remain most dear to God, and they must not be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4).
rite: This feast falls in Denha, the season of the Lord’s dawning, and its theme is the same: the Light shows itself. The feast is also known as the Entrance, for the Lord enters his own house. At each Holy Qurbana we too come to the Temple, and in the Mysteries we receive the same Lord whom Simeon held in his arms. Parents who bring a newborn child to the church for baptism are walking the road of Mary and Joseph. St John Paul II set this day aside in 1997 as the World Day for Consecrated Life, so today the Church also gives thanks for those who, like Anna, have given their lives to God in prayer and service.
study: Mary and Joseph offered what the poor could offer. What small and honest offering can I bring to God today, without being ashamed that it is small?
Isaiah’s Servant does not break the bruised reed. Who around me is a bruised reed, and how do I treat that person?
Paul’s first response to those who did not accept his message was prayer. How do I respond to those who do not share my faith?
Simeon and Anna waited for a lifetime. What helps me to keep hoping when God seems slow?

lead: Two people carry the word today, in very different circumstances. An old apostle in chains hands on his charge: “proclaim the message”. A woman of Samaria, who came for water, leaves her jar at the well and runs to tell her town. Between them stands Jesus, who says that doing the Father’s will is his food, and that the harvest is already ripe. Denha shows Christ to the world, and the world still comes to know him through those who speak of him.

set: This letter is presented as Paul’s last word, written from prison (1:8; 2:9) to Timothy, the younger co-worker he had taken on at Lystra (Acts 16:1–3). Many hold that Paul wrote it or that it rests on his own words; many scholars think that a disciple composed it in his name and spirit after his death. Either way the Church receives it as inspired Scripture, and it reads as a father’s farewell to his son in the faith.
The passage comes straight after the famous words on Scripture (3:16–17). The charge to preach follows from them.
str: vv. 1–2: a solemn charge before God and Christ the Judge.
vv. 3–4: the reason: a time of itching ears.
v. 5: “As for you”: four short commands.
v. 6: “As for me”: the writer’s life is being poured out.
kw: From the word for a herald, who announces a message he did not compose. The preacher’s task is first to hand on what has been entrusted to him, not to display his own ideas.
A wordplay in Greek: “in season, out of season”. Convenience, whether the preacher’s or the hearers’, does not decide when the Gospel is spoken.
I am being poured out as a libation
A libation was wine poured out with a sacrifice (Numbers 28:7). The same verb appears in Philippians 2:17. The writer sees his coming death as an act of worship.
vv: proclaim the message; be persistent whether the time is favorable or unfavorable; convince, rebuke, and encourage, with the utmost patience in teaching.
Three verbs, and only the middle one is harsh. All three are held inside “the utmost patience”. Correction without patience wounds, and patience without truth leaves people where they are.
having itching ears, they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own desires

The danger described lies as much in the listeners as in the teachers. People go looking for voices that say what they already want to hear. The warning applies in every age, and to every side of every argument.
As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation, and the time of my departure has come.
“Departure” (analysis) was used of a ship slipping its moorings or a camp being taken down. Death is spoken of here as setting out, without fear.
ch: The Second Vatican Council, cited by the Catechism, names preaching the Gospel as the first task of bishops, with priests as their co-workers (CCC 888). Lay people share the same mission by word and by the witness of life (CCC 905). St Paul VI wrote that people today listen more willingly to witnesses than to teachers, and if they listen to teachers it is because they are witnesses (Evangelii Nuntiandi 41). Verse 5, “endure suffering”, says the same thing in fewer words.

r.h: My food is to do the will of him who sent me
set: We are at Jacob’s well near Sychar in Samaria, at about noon (4:5–6). The disciples had gone to buy food (4:8), and Jesus has been speaking with a Samaritan woman, to whom he has just said plainly that he is the Messiah (4:25–26). Jews and Samaritans had a long and bitter separation behind them (4:9). It was also not the custom for a teacher to hold such a conversation with a woman in public, which is why the disciples are astonished.

The reading has a double movement. The woman goes into the town while the disciples stay with Jesus and misunderstand him about food. Then the townspeople come out, and Jesus shows the disciples what they are seeing.
str: v. 27: the disciples return; astonished, they say nothing.
vv. 28–30: the woman leaves her jar and speaks to the town; the people set out.
vv. 31–34: “Rabbi, eat something”: his true food.
vv. 35–38: the harvest; sower and reaper.
kw: The same word as the stone jars at Cana (2:6–7). Each time, something is left behind or changed when Jesus is present. She came for this jar’s water, and now she has forgotten it.
The disciples think of bread. As so often in John, a plain word lifts to a higher level: what keeps Jesus alive is the Father’s will.
“To complete his work”. A related word is his last word on the Cross: “It is finished” (19:30). The whole of his life is already in view at this well.
vv: Then the woman left her water jar and went back to the city.
She does not argue or explain. The one who had come to the well at noon now goes to the people of her town, with her question.
“Come and see a man who told me everything I have ever done! He cannot be the Messiah, can he?”
“Come and see” are the words of Philip to Nathanael (1:46). She does not claim to have all the answers. She tells what happened to her and asks a question, and that is enough to start them walking.
My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.
Jesus was tired and thirsty at the start of the chapter (4:6–7). He does not despise bread. He says that there is something he lives by even more.
look around you, and see how the fields are ripe for harvesting.
The Greek says the fields are “white”. Perhaps at that very moment the people of the town are coming across the fields toward him. The harvest is not four months off. It is walking up the road.
ch: The Catechism sees in this well the wonder of prayer itself: Christ comes to meet every human being, and “it is he who first seeks us and asks us for a drink” (CCC 2560). It also teaches that in Christ’s human will the will of the Father was perfectly done (CCC 2824). St Augustine, in his homilies on John, takes the jar she left as a sign of worldly desire laid aside for the sake of living water (in substance). St John Chrysostom admires her as one who did the work of an apostle, drawing a whole town by her words (in substance).

qa: Who are the “others” who have labored, in v. 38?

John does not say. Many readers think of the prophets and John the Baptist; Jesus himself has sown in this very conversation. Some scholars also see in it a look ahead to the later mission to Samaria (Acts 8). The point stays the same: no missionary starts from nothing, and every harvest depends on those who went before.
study: Paul’s charge to Timothy holds truth and patience together. Which of the two do I find harder when I correct someone at home or in the parish?
The Samaritan woman said only what had happened to her and asked a question. To whom could I say, “Come and see”?

lead: Both readings ask us to look at time and at other people as God does. Second Peter answers those who complain that the Lord is slow: his delay is mercy, “the patience of our Lord as salvation”. In the Gospel Jesus asks us to give others the same patience: do not judge, forgive, give, and look first at the log in your own eye. The Church also remembers St John de Britto, who gave his life on Indian soil.

r.h: Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation
set: These are the last lines of the letter. It bears the name of Simon Peter (1:1). Many scholars think that it is among the latest writings of the New Testament, composed by someone in Peter’s tradition, who speaks in his name; others hold to more direct links with the apostle. The Church receives it as Scripture.

The letter answers scoffers who were asking, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (3:4). Its reply is that God’s time is not ours, and that he is patient, “not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (3:9). Our reading draws the conclusion for daily life.
str: v. 14: while you wait, strive to be found at peace.
v. 15a: the delay is salvation.
vv. 15b–16: Paul says the same, and some twist his letters.
v. 17: a warning.
v. 18: grow; and a doxology to Christ.
kw: Literally “long-temper”, the opposite of being quick to anger. The Greek Old Testament uses related words for God’s patience with his people (Exodus 34:6). Every day that the end does not come is a day of mercy.
Used only here in the New Testament. A writer of the New Testament admits that Paul can be difficult. This should comfort every reader who has struggled with Romans or Galatians.

“As they do the other scriptures”: this is an early witness that Paul’s letters were being placed beside the sacred writings. It is one step on the road by which the Church came to discern the canon (CCC 120).
vv: and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation.
We would like the wrong put right at once. The letter reads the delay another way: the time we complain about is also the time in which we ourselves have room to repent.
There are some things in them hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other scriptures.
Difficult is not the same as closed. The warning is against bending the text to suit oneself. This is why the Church reads Scripture within the living Tradition (Dei Verbum 10, 12).
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
The letter ends with a command that keeps the reader moving. The opposite of being carried away (v. 17) is growing. Grace and knowledge go together.
ch: The Catechism quotes this letter’s words about God’s patience when it teaches that God predestines no one to hell, and that the Church implores the mercy of God, who does not want “any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (CCC 1037, citing 2 Peter 3:9). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the task of authentically interpreting the word of God has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church, which serves the word and does not stand above it (Dei Verbum 10; CCC 85–86).

r.h: Do not judge, and you will not be judged
set: This is part of Luke’s Sermon on the Plain (6:17–49), which has much in common with Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount. Jesus has just taught love of enemies, ending with the words, “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (6:36). Today’s reading shows what that mercy looks like when we deal with those around us.
str: vv. 37–38: four commands and the image of the measure.
vv. 39–40: the blind guide; a disciple and his teacher.
vv. 41–42: the speck and the log.
kw: The usual meaning of this verb is to release or let go. To forgive is to stop holding someone in our debt.

The fold of a long garment above the belt, used like a large pocket. The picture is of a grain seller who presses down and shakes the measure so that it holds as much as possible, and then lets it spill over. “Will be put” is literally “they will give”, a Semitic way of speaking that here most likely means God.
A chip of wood or a bit of straw, and a beam that holds up a roof. A carpenter from Nazareth would have known both. The exaggeration is deliberate and a little comic.
vv: Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven;
Two prohibitions, then two positive commands: “Forgive” and, in v. 38, “give”. The passive verbs quietly name God as the one who judges and forgives.
for the measure you give will be the measure you get back.
We set the scale ourselves. God’s generosity far outruns ours, as the overflowing lap shows, but a closed hand cannot receive.
Why do you see the speck in your neighbor’s eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?
The fault of another is easy to see because it is the size of a speck, and my own is hard to see because it is too close to me.
You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor’s eye.
Jesus does not say the speck should stay. He says “first”. A person who has faced his own sin can help a brother gently. Hypokritēs was the Greek word for a stage actor.
ch: The Catechism warns against rash judgment, which assumes a neighbor’s moral fault without sufficient foundation (CCC 2477), and quotes St Ignatius of Loyola: every good Christian should be more ready to give a favorable interpretation to another’s statement than to condemn it (CCC 2478). St Augustine sees in the speck and the log the difference between anger, which can pass, and hatred, which has grown old in the heart (in substance).

qa: If I must not judge, may I never say that something is wrong?

Jesus is not forbidding us to tell right from wrong; he expects the speck to be removed. The Catechism gives the distinction: we can judge that an act is in itself gravely wrong, but we must entrust the judgment of persons to the justice and mercy of God (CCC 1861). We can name a sin without passing sentence on a soul.
rite: St John de Britto (1647–1693), born in Lisbon and brought up at the royal court, gave up that life to serve as a Jesuit in the Madurai mission. He lived as a simple Indian ascetic, a pandaraswami, spoke Tamil, and was known to the people as Arul Anandar. Expelled once and invited to stay in Portugal, he came back. He was beheaded at Oriyur in the Marava country on 4 February 1693, and Pope Pius XII canonized him in 1947. The Madurai mission lies not far from our own land. His life gives flesh to today’s Gospel: he gave a good measure, pressed down and running over. Those who suffer for the faith in many lands today are in our prayer, with all who have wronged them.
study: When has God’s “delay” in my life turned out to be mercy, for me or for someone else?
Whom do I judge most quickly? What is the log in my own eye that I would rather not look at?

lead: On the Fridays of Denha the Church remembers those through whom Christ has been made known. On this last Friday before the Great Fast she remembers all the faithful departed, so that we enter the fast in communion with the whole family of God. Ezekiel sees a valley of dry bones and hears God ask whether they can live. Sirach praises the ancestors, including those whom no one remembers any more. Paul speaks of the dead as seed sown in hope. In Matthew the King gathers the nations and blesses those who served him without knowing it. Four words carry the readings: breath, memory, seed and the least.

set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC (1:1–3). News of the fall of Jerusalem reached him in exile (33:21), after the city was destroyed in 587/586 BC. The people had lost the land, the king and the Temple. Their despair is quoted in v. 11: “Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost”.

The vision is God’s answer. In its first meaning it promises that the nation will be raised up and brought home (vv. 12, 14). It is not yet a direct teaching about the resurrection of each person, a faith that became clear later in Israel (Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7). But the power that it shows, of God bringing life out of death, is what that later faith would rest on. Jewish tradition treasured this passage too: it is painted on the wall of the third-century synagogue at Dura-Europos in Syria.
str: vv. 1–2: the valley and the very dry bones.
v. 3: God’s question and the prophet’s answer.
vv. 4–6: the command to prophesy to the bones.
vv. 7–8: bones, sinews, flesh, skin, but no breath.
vv. 9–10: prophecy to the breath: they live and stand.
vv. 11–14: God’s explanation: the graves opened, the Spirit given.
kw: One Hebrew word which the NRSV translates in three ways. It comes ten times in these fourteen verses. The vision depends on the word. What comes from “the four winds” (v. 9) to give breath is finally “my spirit” (v. 14).
Literally “son of man”, as the Malayalam POC keeps it. The phrase stresses human frailty, and God addresses Ezekiel with it throughout the book. A mortal standing among the dead is told to speak.
“Our hope is lost” (v. 11). The word is not a mood but a thing that a people has or loses. God does not answer the despair by denying it. He says, “I am going to open your graves”.
vv: He said to me, “Mortal, can these bones live?” I answered, “O Lord God, you know.”
An honest answer, and a humble one. Ezekiel does not say yes, because he can see the bones. He does not say no, because he knows who is asking.
and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood on their feet, a vast multitude.
The two stages recall Genesis 2:7, where God first forms the man from the dust and then breathes into him. What happens in this valley is a new creation.
They say, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are cut off completely.’
Those who grieve and those who have lost heart will know these words. God takes them seriously and quotes them back.
I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live,
The sinews and skin are not the end. Only God’s own Spirit gives life. Jesus’ breathing on the disciples on Easter evening (John 20:22) stands in this same line.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God revealed the resurrection of the dead to his people progressively (CCC 992), and it counts Ezekiel 37 among the prophetic texts about the sending of the Spirit (CCC 715). St Irenaeus uses this passage to answer those who denied the resurrection of the flesh: the God who first formed us from the dust can raise the same body again (Against Heresies, Book 5; in substance). Reading it at a commemoration of the dead, the Church hears a promise for those who sleep in the graves of our parishes.

set: Jesus Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, and his grandson later translated the book into Greek in Egypt (see the prologue). It is among the books the Catholic Church receives as canonical, and it has been called Ecclesiasticus, “the Church’s book”, because of its long use in teaching. Chapters 44–50 are a long hymn in praise of the great figures of Israel, from Enoch and Noah to the high priest Simon of Ben Sira’s own time.

Today’s reading is the introduction to that hymn. It praises rulers, counsellors, prophets and poets, and it then does something unexpected: it remembers those who have left no memory at all. Ben Sira’s hope for the dead rests on their good name and their descendants. He has not yet the clear hope of resurrection found in Paul’s letter today. The two readings need each other.
str: vv. 1–2: the call to praise.
vv. 3–6: the kinds of people who are praised.
vv. 7–8: those honoured in their own time.
v. 9: those with no memorial.
vv. 10–13: yet their righteousness lasts, in their children.
vv. 14–15: buried in peace; their name lives.
kw: “Of others there is no memory” (v. 9). The Greek word is what is left to keep someone in mind, a tomb or a name. Ben Sira admits how quickly most human lives are forgotten.

Literally “men of mercy”, and behind the Greek stands the Hebrew ḥesed, faithful love. So the Malayalam POC speaks of the merciful. Those whom no one remembers are praised for what they were toward others.
“Their name lives on generation after generation” (v. 14). In the Bible a name is the person himself. Baptism gives us a name by which God calls us (Isaiah 43:1).
vv: Let us now sing the praises of famous men, our ancestors in their generations.
“Ancestors” here is literally “fathers”, but we rightly think today of the mothers too, in the many generations who handed on the faith.
But of others there is no memory; they have perished as though they had never existed;
It is a plain and painful line. Most of our great-great-grandparents are known to no one on earth.
But these also were godly men, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten;
Forgotten by us, not by God. Those whose names we have lost are the reason a Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed exists.
Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives on generation after generation.
Compare the burial prayer that many Christians know: “may they rest in peace”. The peace of the grave is not the last thing said of them.
ch: The Catechism teaches, in the words of the Second Vatican Council, that from the earliest times the Church has honoured the memory of the dead and offered prayers for them (CCC 958; Lumen Gentium 50). In praying for all the faithful departed she includes those who have no one left to pray for them.

set: Some in the church at Corinth were saying, “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). Greek thinking often looked for the soul’s escape from the body, and the idea of a body rising seemed foolish to many. Paul has answered with the Resurrection of Christ (15:1–28). Now he takes up the practical question, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” (15:35), and begins with the image of a seed (15:36–38).
His argument is that God makes many kinds of bodies, so the risen body need not be just like this one. It is this body, changed. It stands to the present body as a plant stands to its seed.
str: vv. 39–41: many kinds of flesh and of glory.
vv. 42–44a: four contrasts: sown and raised.
vv. 44b–46: physical and spiritual, in that order.
vv. 47–49: the two Adams, and whose image we shall bear.
kw: The word comes four times in vv. 42–44. Paul is thinking of burial as sowing. The early Christians buried their dead as a farmer puts seed in the ground, in expectation.

This pair is often misunderstood. “Spiritual” here does not mean made of no matter. It means a body wholly given life by the Spirit of God, as the present body is given life by the natural soul (psychē).
Genesis 1:26–27 says humankind is made in God’s image. Christ is the perfect image, and the destiny of the baptized is to bear that image in the body as well.
vv: What is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness, it is raised in power.
Anyone who has stood at a grave knows what dishonor and weakness are. Paul does not deny them. He says that they are not the end of the story.
It is sown a physical body, it is raised a spiritual body.
“It” is the same in both clauses. The one who is raised is the one who was buried, not someone else.
“The first man, Adam, became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
Paul quotes Genesis 2:7. Adam received breath; the risen Christ gives it. The valley of Ezekiel 37 is fulfilled in this verse.
Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we will also bear the image of the man of heaven.

A note on the text. Most ancient manuscripts, including P46, read “let us bear”, a call to live now as those who belong to Christ. A smaller number read “we will bear”, which the NRSV and the Malayalam POC follow as better suiting the argument. The difference in Greek is one vowel. Both are true: what we shall be, we must begin to live.
ch: The Catechism says that the “how” of the resurrection exceeds our imagination and understanding, and that it is accessible only to faith (CCC 1000). It teaches that we believe in “the true resurrection of this flesh that we now possess” (CCC 1017), and that Christ is raised with his own body, and “all of them will rise again with their own bodies” (CCC 999). St Augustine, in The City of God (Book 22), explains the spiritual body as true flesh, wholly and gladly subject to the spirit (in substance).

r.h: Just as you did it to one of the least of these
set: This is the last great scene of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew, just before the Passion narrative begins (26:1–2). The Son of Man of Daniel 7:13–14 comes in glory, and he is also called “the king” (v. 34) and pictured as a shepherd, as in Ezekiel 34:17. The Church reads only the blessing today, vv. 31–40. The sentence on those at the left follows in vv. 41–46.

In that part of the world sheep and goats often grazed together and were separated at the end of the day. In this scene the separation turns not on what people could say about the King but on how they treated him without knowing it. This does not make faith unimportant: the same Gospel calls all nations to discipleship and baptism (28:19–20).
str: vv. 31–33: the King on his throne; the sheep and the goats.
vv. 34–36: “Come, you that are blessed”, and six works of mercy.
vv. 37–39: the surprise of the righteous.
v. 40: the King’s answer.
kw: The judgment reaches all people, not Israel or the Church alone.
The Greek superlative of “small”. Those named are the hungry, thirsty, strangers, naked, sick and imprisoned.

Literally “brothers”. Some scholars think that in Matthew’s first setting these are Christ’s disciples and missionaries (compare 10:40–42; 12:48–50), while others read the phrase as covering all who are in need. The Church in her teaching applies it to all the poor (CCC 544, 2443–2449).
vv: Then the king will say to those at his right hand, ‘Come, you that are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world;
The kingdom was prepared long before they did anything. It is an inheritance, a gift of the Father, and they receive it as children receive what is theirs.
for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,

He does not say that they gave food to “the poor”. He says “me”. The list that continues in v. 36 has six works, and Christian tradition, recalling Tobit 1:17–18, adds a seventh: burying the dead (CCC 2447). So today’s commemoration belongs here too.
‘Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food, or thirsty and gave you something to drink?
They are astonished. They did not do good by keeping count, and they do not remember doing anything great. Love that is real does not keep accounts.
‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.’
“One” is enough. No one has to feed the world. Each person is asked about the one who was at the door.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus identifies himself with the poor of every kind and makes active love toward them the condition for entering his kingdom (CCC 544). It teaches that our attitude to our neighbor will disclose acceptance or refusal of grace and divine love on the last day (CCC 678), and it quotes St John of the Cross: “At the evening of life, we shall be judged on our love” (CCC 1022). St John Chrysostom says to those who would honour Christ’s Body in the church: do not neglect him outside, where he is cold and naked (Homilies on Matthew, 50; in substance). The same Father urges us to help the dead with our prayers and offerings (CCC 1032).

qa: Does Ezekiel 37 teach the resurrection of the body?

In its first meaning it promises the restoration of the exiled nation, as v. 11 says plainly. It was natural, later, for Jews and Christians to read it of the resurrection, because the God who can do this for a people can do it for a person. God revealed the resurrection gradually (CCC 992), and the full light came with Christ.
Paul says “spiritual body”. Does that mean we rise as spirits or ghosts?

No. The risen Jesus said, “a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). Paul’s “spiritual” means fully alive with the Spirit of God. We shall rise as ourselves, body and soul, transformed and no longer subject to death.
If each person is judged at death, why do we pray for the dead?

The Church teaches that those who die in God’s friendship but are not yet fully purified undergo a purification before entering heaven, and that from the beginning she has honoured them and prayed for them, above all in the Eucharistic sacrifice (CCC 1030–1032). She bases this on Scripture (the Catechism cites 2 Maccabees 12) and on her constant practice. Love does not stop at the grave.
rite: The East Syriac tradition gives the Fridays of Denha to the great witnesses of the faith and closes the series with all the faithful departed. So the season’s last Friday looks at those through whom the faith reached us: parents, grandparents, catechists and priests. Many families will pray and light candles at the graves of their dead, and each Holy Qurbana offered for them joins them to the one offering of Christ. The Great Fast begins next Monday, and it is fitting to enter it with our dead in mind, asking pardon for what we owe them and thanking God for what we received from them.
study: Ezekiel answers, “O Lord God, you know.” What situation in my family or my parish looks to me like a valley of dry bones? How can I pray that honest prayer over it?
Who are the forgotten people to whom I owe my faith? Is there someone in my family for whom no one prays any more?
Paul speaks of burial as sowing. How would that image change the way I speak to a child about death?
Who is “the least” at my own door this week? What is one work of mercy I can do during the coming Great Fast?

lead: This is the last Saturday before the Great Fast, and both readings speak of need. The rich church of Laodicea says, “I need nothing”, and Christ stands outside its door and knocks. The crowds in Galilee know exactly what they need, and they lay their sick at his feet. The readings ask which of these two we resemble as the fast draws near.

r.h: I am standing at the door, knocking
set: This is the last of the seven letters to the churches of Asia (Revelation 2–3). Laodicea stood in the Lycus valley in what is now western Turkey, near Hierapolis and Colossae (Colossians 4:13). It was a wealthy city. The Roman historian Tacitus records that after an earthquake in the reign of Nero it rebuilt itself from its own resources, without help from Rome (Annals 14.27).

Many commentators also see local colour in the letter. The city was known for banking, for its woollen cloth, and for a medical school linked with a famous eye remedy, which would give point to the gold, the white robes and the salve of v. 18. Many think too that “lukewarm” recalls its water supply, brought in by aqueduct, in contrast with the hot springs of Hierapolis and the cool water of Colossae. These are scholars’ suggestions, though well founded.
str: v. 14: the titles of the One who speaks.
vv. 15–16: neither cold nor hot.
vv. 17–18: “I am rich”, and his counsel.
vv. 19–20: love, repentance, the knock at the door.
vv. 21–22: the promise to the one who conquers.
kw: Found only here in the Bible. Many commentators do not take “cold” as bad and “hot” as good, as feelings go. Hot and cold water are both useful, while lukewarm water is of no use and makes one retch. On this reading the reproach is about a faith that does no one any good.

A title of Christ, perhaps echoing “the God of faithfulness” in the Hebrew of Isaiah 65:16, where the word is ’āmēn. He is God’s own firm and reliable word. Laodicea’s words about itself are false; his are true.
The verb for the main meal of the day, at evening, when friends sit long together. Deipnon is the word Paul uses for “the Lord’s supper” (1 Corinthians 11:20).
vv: So, because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am about to spit you out of my mouth.
A hard image, and yet the letter is not closing the door. The verb means “I am about to”, and everything that follows is an offer.
For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing.’ You do not realize that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.
The sickness is that they do not know they are ill. The other letters speak of persecution and false teaching. This one, which has no word of praise, speaks of contentment.
I reprove and discipline those whom I love. Be earnest, therefore, and repent.
He echoes Proverbs 3:12. The harshest letter of the seven contains the plainest word of love.
Listen! I am standing at the door, knocking; if you hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to you and eat with you, and you with me.
This is said to a church, a baptized community, and he is outside it. He does not break the door down. Hearing comes first, and then the meal.
ch: The Catechism says that God tirelessly calls each person to the mysterious encounter of prayer, and that it is he who takes the first step (CCC 2567). St Ambrose, commenting on the Psalms, says that blessed is the one at whose door Christ knocks, and that our door is faith (in substance). St John Paul II began his pontificate in 1978 with the words, “Open wide the doors for Christ”. Those who gather for the Holy Qurbana can hear in “eat with you” the promise that is kept at the Lord’s table.

set: Matthew has just told of Jesus in the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed the daughter of a Canaanite woman (15:21–28). Now he returns to the Sea of Galilee and goes up a mountain, and soon he will feed four thousand people (15:32–39). Mark places this period of his work in the Decapolis, a largely Gentile area (Mark 7:31). For that reason, and because the crowd praises “the God of Israel”, many scholars think Matthew means us to picture Gentiles among the crowd. The text does not say so directly.
str: v. 29: Jesus goes up the mountain and sits.
v. 30: the crowds lay their sick at his feet, and he cures them.
v. 31: amazement and praise.
kw: A strong verb, whose ordinary meaning is “threw” or “cast down”. One can imagine the crush and the urgency. There is not much ceremony in this scene.
Kyllos is someone with a damaged limb. Hygiēs is the word from which “hygiene” comes, meaning sound and healthy. The crowd sees what had been broken made whole.
vv: he went up the mountain, where he sat down.
To sit was the posture of a teacher, as at the start of the Sermon on the Mount (5:1). On this mountain he teaches by healing.
Great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the maimed, the blind, the mute, and many others. They put them at his feet, and he cured them,
Most of the sick here cannot reach him alone. Someone carries them. All the work of the crowd is in the carrying, and Matthew reports the rest in three plain words.
so that the crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the maimed whole, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they praised the God of Israel.

The list recalls Isaiah 35:5–6: “then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy.” The prophet’s promise for the day of God’s coming is taking place on this hillside.
ch: The Catechism calls Jesus’ healings messianic signs, by which he delivered some from earthly evils in order to deliver people from the gravest evil, sin (CCC 549), and it says that his compassion for the sick is a resplendent sign that “God has visited his people” (CCC 1503). The Church continues this care in the Anointing of the Sick and in every family and hospital where the sick are brought to Christ in prayer and tended with love.

qa: How can Christ call a church “lukewarm” and also say he loves it?

He says both in the same breath: “I reprove and discipline those whom I love” (3:19). His reproach is that of a physician or a parent, not of an enemy. A warning given while there is still time to change is itself a mercy.
study: In what part of my life do I say, “I need nothing”? What would it mean to open that door as the Great Fast begins?
The sick in the Gospel were carried by others. Whom can I carry to Christ in prayer or in care this week?

lead: With this Sunday the Church stands at the door of the Great Fast, the fifty days that lead to the Pasha of the Lord. The four readings together explain what a fast is for. Moses spends forty days with God, and his face shines without his knowing it. Isaiah warns that a fast without justice is empty, and he describes the fast God actually wants. Paul speaks of taking off an old self like a garment and clothing ourselves with a new one. In the Gospel Jesus, led by the Spirit, fasts forty days in the wilderness and overcomes the tempter with the word of God. The readings run from a shining face to a shared loaf, to a new garment, to victory, and their key words are presence, justice, renewal and the word.

set: The people have made the golden calf (Exodus 32), Moses has broken the first tablets (32:19), and he has pleaded for them (32:30–32; 33:12–17). In chapter 34 God renews the covenant and gives new tablets. Today’s reading is the close of that story. After the worst sin of the desert, God is still speaking with his people, and his glory now shows on the face of the mediator.
Deuteronomy tells of the same forty days without food and water (Deuteronomy 9:9, 18). They are not a work Moses does to win something from God. He is so taken up with God that he does not eat.
str: vv. 27–28: the covenant words, and the forty days.
vv. 29–30: Moses comes down, and the people are afraid.
vv. 31–32: he calls them near and gives them the commandments.
vv. 33–35: the custom of the veil.
kw: An unusual verb, related to the noun qeren, “horn”, perhaps because rays looked like horns. St Jerome’s Latin rendered it “horned”, which is why Michelangelo’s statue of Moses and many medieval pictures show him with horns.
Literally “the ten words”. This is the source of the name Decalogue. Commandment here is a word of the living God, spoken within a covenant.

Found in the Bible only in these verses. Its use is curious: Moses is unveiled before God and when he speaks God’s word to the people, and he covers his face at other times. Paul will make much of this veil (2 Corinthians 3:7–18).
vv: He was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water.
Forty recalls the time of testing and meeting God. Elijah walks forty days to the same mountain (1 Kings 19:8), and Jesus fasts forty days in today’s Gospel.
Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.

This is the heart of the reading. He did not know. Holiness that knows it is shining is usually doing something else. The fast has not made Moses admire himself. It has left something on his face that others can see.
When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil on his face;
Being close to God does not separate Moses from the people. He comes back, calls them near (v. 31), and hands on the word. What he received on the mountain was for them.
ch: St Paul reads this passage and says, “all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). On the mountain of the Transfiguration Jesus’ “face shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2), with Moses and Elijah beside him. The Catechism notes that Moses drew strength and determination for his intercession from this intimacy with God (CCC 2577). The Great Fast aims at this sort of nearness.

set: Many scholars attribute chapters 56–66 of Isaiah to the period after the return from exile (from 538 BC), when the community was struggling to rebuild. It was keeping fasts of mourning for the destruction of Jerusalem (Zechariah 7:5). People were devout, yet social wrongs continued, and they wondered why God did not respond.

The chapter is a prophetic challenge from within Israel’s own faith. Israel’s prophets, whose words Israel preserved, spoke like this to their own people. Jesus stands in this line (Matthew 6:16–18), and the same challenge is addressed to the Church today.
str: vv. 1–2: the prophet’s commission, and a people who appear devout.
v. 3a: the people’s complaint.
vv. 3b–5: God’s answer: what is wrong with this fast.
vv. 6–7: the fast God chooses.
vv. 8–10: the promises: light, healing, an answer.
kw: The ordinary word for fasting from food. The prophet is not abolishing it, as the rest of Scripture shows. He is asking what it is joined to.
The verb means to split or burst open, the way dawn splits the night. It is the same image as “your light shall rise in the darkness” (v. 10).
Literally “from your own flesh”. It could mean one’s relatives, and the fuller sense also reaches all who share our flesh. Sometimes the hardest almsgiving is reconciliation within the family.
vv: “Why do we fast, but you do not see? Why humble ourselves, but you do not notice?” Look, you serve your own interest on your fast day, and oppress all your workers.
They treat fasting as a way to get God’s attention. The answer turns their gaze from heaven to the people who work for them.
Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice, to undo the thongs of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?
Four verbs of release. The yoke is an image of someone’s labour being taken from him by force. A fast that leaves another person’s burden in place is not yet the fast God wants.
Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover them, and not to hide yourself from your own kin?
“Your bread”: what I do not eat in the fast is meant for someone. Note that this is close to the list in Matthew 25:35–36.
Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up quickly;
The one who looks after others’ wounds finds his own healed. God is no longer asked to “see”: now, “you shall call, and the Lord will answer” (v. 9).
if you offer your food to the hungry and satisfy the needs of the afflicted, then your light shall rise in the darkness and your gloom be like the noonday.
The same word that promised light in v. 8 closes the reading. Light is what the fast is for, and it comes through the hungry.
ch: The Catechism says that Scripture and the Fathers insist above all on three forms of penance: fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434), and it names the seasons and days of penance, among them Lent, as intense moments of the Church’s penitential practice (CCC 1438). St Peter Chrysologus says that fasting is the soul of prayer, and mercy is the lifeblood of fasting; these three are one, and cannot be separated (in substance). St John Chrysostom asks those who fast to prove it by their works, and to let eyes, ears, hands and feet fast too (in substance).

r.h: Clothe yourselves with the new self
set: The letter presents itself as written by Paul in prison (3:1; 4:1). Many hold that it is his; many scholars think that it was composed by a disciple who gathered his teaching. Chapters 1–3 tell what God has done in Christ. From 4:1 on, the letter says how those who have received it are to live.

The readers are Gentile converts, and when the letter says “as the Gentiles live” it is telling them not to go back to the life they had left. It is not a judgment on every person outside the Church, or on our neighbours of other faiths. The Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2).
str: vv. 17–19: the old way of life, darkened and without feeling.
vv. 20–21: “That is not the way you learned Christ!”
vv. 22–24: taking off, being renewed, clothing.
kw: Emptiness, the condition of a life aimed at nothing that lasts. The Greek Old Testament uses it for “vanity of vanities” in Ecclesiastes 1:2.

Words for taking off and putting on clothes. They probably reflect the early practice of baptism, in which the candidate took off his garments and was clothed in white after coming out of the water (compare Galatians 3:27; Colossians 3:9–10).
Unlike the verbs for putting off and putting on, this one is in the present tense in Greek, and the renewal is ongoing. The clothes were changed once at baptism, but the mind is renewed every day.
vv: That is not the way you learned Christ!
An unusual phrase. Paul does not say “learned about Christ”, as one learns a subject. To become a Christian is to learn a person, and that lesson shows in how a person lives.
You were taught to put away your former way of life, your old self, corrupt and deluded by its lusts,
“Old self” is literally “old man”, as the POC keeps it. It is not one bad habit but a whole way of being. Its desires promise much and deceive.
and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,
The Great Fast is not only about the stomach. What changes is the way we see.
and to clothe yourselves with the new self, created according to the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
“Created” speaks of what only God can do, as in Genesis 1. Our new self is not self-improvement. It is a new creation, and it is given. We are asked to put it on.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the white garment of baptism signifies that the baptized person has “put on Christ” (CCC 1243), and it cites this verse when it says that the Christian must strive to put off the old man and put on the new man (CCC 1473). St Leo the Great, preaching at the start of the fast, says that what a Christian should be doing at all times should now be done with greater care and devotion (in substance). The Second Vatican Council names the recalling of baptism, or the preparation for it, and penance as the two marks of this season (Sacrosanctum Concilium 109).

set: Immediately before this the voice from heaven has said, “This is my Son, the Beloved” (3:17). The devil’s first words question exactly that: “If you are the Son of God”. Jesus is led into the wilderness not by the devil but by the Spirit.

The scene recalls Israel in the desert, God’s “firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1, which Matthew quotes in 2:15). Israel was tested forty years, and Deuteronomy 8:2 says that God led the people so as to humble and test them. Jesus answers all three temptations from Deuteronomy 6–8, the chapters in which Moses reflects on that time. He relives his people’s story from within, as one of them, and remains faithful. Matthew’s order ends on a mountain; Luke’s ends at the Temple (Luke 4:1–13).
str: vv. 1–2: the Spirit, the wilderness, forty days.
vv. 3–4: stones into bread: Deuteronomy 8:3.
vv. 5–7: the pinnacle of the Temple: Psalm 91 misused, and Deuteronomy 6:16.
vv. 8–10: all the kingdoms: Deuteronomy 6:13.
v. 11: the devil leaves; angels come.
kw: The same Greek verb means both. God tests in order to strengthen; the devil tempts in order to destroy. The same event can be both, depending on who is at work (CCC 2846–2847).

The Greek perfect tense: it was written and it stands. Jesus says it three times. The tempter also quotes Scripture (v. 6), so simply quoting a text is not enough. It must be read with the mind of God.
The devil asks for this in v. 9. The Magi offered it to the child in 2:11, and the disciples will offer it to the risen Lord on another mountain in 28:17.
vv: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
The same Spirit who came upon him at the baptism leads him here. Temptation is not a sign that God has gone away.
He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was famished.
Matthew adds “and forty nights”, as with Moses (Exodus 34:28). He does not hide the hunger. The Son of God is truly human, and he is tempted at the point of his real need.
“It is written, ‘One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”
Bread is not the problem, and Jesus will soon multiply it (14:13–21). The temptation is to use his power for himself. He will live on what his Father gives, as Israel lived on manna.
“Again it is written, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
Forcing God’s hand with a spectacle is not trust but its opposite. The devil quotes Psalm 91 and misses its real point, which is quiet confidence.
“Away with you, Satan! for it is written, ‘Worship the Lord your God, and serve only him.’”

The tempter offers all the kingdoms for one act of worship. On a mountain at the end of the Gospel Jesus will say, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (28:18). It comes from the Father and by way of the Cross.
Then the devil left him, and suddenly angels came and waited on him.
The verb is “served”, or “ministered”. The very help the devil tried to demand in v. 6 is now given when it is not demanded.
ch: The Catechism explains that Jesus is the new Adam who remained faithful where the first Adam gave in to temptation, and that he fulfils Israel’s vocation perfectly (CCC 539). “By the solemn forty days of Lent the Church unites herself each year to the mystery of Jesus in the desert” (CCC 540). It teaches that this victory is won through prayer (CCC 2849). St Augustine says in his commentary on the Psalms that Christ made us one with him when he was tempted, so that in him you were tempted and in him you overcome (in substance).

qa: Why is Moses shown with horns in some paintings and statues?

The Hebrew verb for “shone” in Exodus 34:29 is related to the word for “horn”, and St Jerome’s Latin translated it “horned”. Artists followed this. The Scripture itself speaks of light. This is an example of why the Church encourages study of the original languages (Dei Verbum 22).
How could Jesus be tempted, if he was without sin?

Temptation is not sin. Jesus was truly tempted from outside by the devil, and he truly felt hunger, yet he never consented. The Letter to the Hebrews says that he “in every respect has been tested as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). This is why he can help us when we are tempted (CCC 540).
Is the Great Fast only about food?

Fasting from food is a real part of it, and the Church has rules for it that each eparchy gives; the sick, the very old and small children are not asked to fast in the same way. But Isaiah 58 and the Fathers insist that the fast must go together with prayer, almsgiving, reconciliation and justice. A fast that leaves the heart unchanged has missed its purpose.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar Church the Great Fast, Sauma Ramba, is the fast of fifty days, counted from this Sunday; the fasting begins tomorrow, Monday, a day of fasting and abstinence on which ashes are blessed in many parishes. Tonight is Pethurtha, the threshold of the fast, kept in our families as a time of reconciliation and of a simple last festive meal. Isaiah’s “your own kin” (58:7) has a sharp point this evening: the fast begins well in a house where old quarrels have been forgiven. At the Holy Qurbana today we pray with Christ, who overcomes in the wilderness and who feeds us with “every word that comes from the mouth of God” and with his own Body and Blood.
study: Moses did not know his face was shining. What would it mean for me to come closer to God during this fast without watching myself do it?
Isaiah says, “share your bread with the hungry”. What will I give up this fast, and who will receive what I give up?
Which “old self” does Ephesians 4 ask me to take off? Is there a particular habit, resentment or way of seeing that I will bring to confession?
Jesus answered the tempter from Scripture. Which verse of the Bible will I keep with me through the fifty days?

lead: The Great Fast opens with the first page of the Bible and with a word about the altar. Genesis shows God speaking light and order into a formless dark, and calling what he makes good. Joshua stands at the edge of the Jordan and hears, “Be strong and courageous”, while Paul in Romans names the old disorder: people served the creature instead of the Creator. In Matthew, Jesus carries the commandment down into the heart, and sends the worshipper away from the altar to make peace first. On the day of Vibhoodi, the ash says that we are dust, and these readings say what God does with dust and darkness. The key words are good, fulfil and reconcile.

set: The Bible opens not with a theory but with a solemn, almost liturgical poem of seven days. Many scholars think this page took its final form among priests in the time of the exile in Babylon, in the sixth century BC, when the great temples and star-gods of the conquerors seemed to rule the world. The Babylonian creation story tells of battles among gods. Genesis has no battle. One God speaks, and it is so. Today's reading covers the first four days and stops before living creatures appear.
str: vv. 1–2: the beginning; the formless void, the dark, the wind from God.
vv. 3–5: day one: light.
vv. 6–8: day two: the dome and the waters.
vv. 9–13: day three: dry land and plants.
vv. 14–19: day four: the lights in the dome of the sky.
¶ There is a pattern. The first three days make spaces out of the void. The next three fill them, and day four fills what day one began. The refrain “And God saw that it was good” sets the rhythm.
kw: In the Old Testament this verb has only God as its subject. The Bible uses it for an act that belongs to God alone.
A rhyming Hebrew phrase for what is empty and without shape. It describes the state before God's ordering word, not a rival power.

Rûaḥ means wind, breath and spirit. The NRSV says “wind”; the Malayalam POC has “spirit of God”, and the Fathers saw here the Holy Spirit. The verb for “swept over” returns in Deuteronomy 32:11, where an eagle “hovers over its young”.
vv: In the beginning when God created the heavens and the earth,
Nothing stands before God. The Church reads the whole page with 2 Maccabees 7:28, where a mother tells her son that God “did not make them out of things that existed”.
Then God said, “Let there be light”; and there was light.

God's first act is a word. Paul remembers this verse when he says that the God who spoke light has now “shone in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 4:6). It is the hope of the Fast: the same word can speak over the dark places in us.
God made the two great lights

Genesis does not use the ordinary Hebrew words for sun and moon, which in neighbouring languages were also names of gods. It says only “the greater light” and “the lesser light”. Lamps hung up by their Maker are not to be worshipped. Paul's complaint in today's epistle, that people “served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25), is the same warning.
And God saw that it was good.
The refrain answers any contempt for the world. We fast from good things, not from bad ones. Food is not the enemy; the fast teaches us who gave it.
ch: The Catechism says that Scripture presents the Creator's work “symbolically as a succession of six days” (CCC 337), and that the world began when God's word drew it out of nothingness (CCC 338). It also joins the Word and the Breath of God at the origin of every creature (CCC 703). St Basil, preaching on these days, reports what he learned from a Syrian: that in his language the verb of 1:2 suggests a bird warming her eggs with her wings, so that the Spirit gives the waters life (in substance). The Syriac-speaking world has been reading this page with love from the beginning.

set: The Sermon on the Mount is the first of five great discourses in Matthew. After the Beatitudes, vv. 17–20 state its principle: Jesus has come to fulfil the law. Then follow six contrasts, “You have heard that it was said... But I say to you”. Today's reading gives the principle and the first contrast, on murder and anger.
str: vv. 17–19: not to abolish but to fulfil.
v. 20: a righteousness that goes further.
vv. 21–22: not only murder, but anger and insult.
vv. 23–24: the gift left before the altar.
vv. 25–26: settle on the way to court.
kw: To fill full. Jesus does not cancel the law but brings it to the goal it was aiming at, and the reader of Matthew has been shown this since 1:22.
The smallest Greek letter and a tiny mark in writing. The POC's “വള്ളിയോ പുള്ളിയോ” catches the same picture.
From the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, remembered for the shameful sacrifices of Jeremiah 7:31. It became an image of final judgment.
vv: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

Many Pharisees were earnest teachers who loved the law, and Jesus does not ask for less than they did. He asks for more: a goodness that reaches the heart. The warning is addressed to his own disciples.
But I say to you that if you are angry with a brother or sister, you will be liable to judgment;

A note on the text. Some ancient manuscripts add “without cause” after “brother”; the NRSV and the POC follow those that lack it. The sentence is stronger without the escape. The word often printed as raka, which the NRSV gives as “insult”, is probably an Aramaic term of contempt, something like “empty head”. No one is to be treated as worthless.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.

Note who has the grievance: not “you have something against your brother” but “your brother or sister has something against you”. The first step belongs to the one who remembers. Jesus' first hearers in Galilee were days from the Temple, so the picture of walking home and back is deliberately striking.
Truly I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
The “penny” is the kodrantēs, a very small Roman coin. A quarrel left alone grows more costly.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus adds to the commandment the prohibition of anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262), and it lists reconciliation before the offering among the first things his teaching on prayer requires (CCC 2608). On Jesus and the law see CCC 577–582. A very early Christian writing, the Didache (14:2), applies the verse to Sunday worship: no one who has a quarrel is to join the assembly until reconciled, so that the sacrifice may not be profaned (in substance).

qa: Does Genesis 1 compete with science?

No. The Catechism calls the six days a symbolic presentation (CCC 337) and welcomes scientific study of the origins of the world (CCC 283–284).
