Genesis answers who made the world, why, and what it is worth. St Augustine warned Christians long ago not to speak foolishly about nature in the name of Scripture (in substance).
rite: The calendar keeps this day as Vibhoodi, a penitential service, with fasting and abstinence from meat. The ash, traditionally from burning last year's Oshana palms, recalls the word to Adam: “you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). In the Holy Qurbana the peace is exchanged before the anaphora begins, so that this Gospel is acted out every time we approach the altar.
study: Who has something against me today, and what is the first step I could take this week?
Which good thing, given by God, have I let take the Creator's place? What might the Fast do about it?

lead: Yesterday's reading stopped at the fourth day; today Genesis reaches the living creatures and man, formed from dust and given God's breath. In the second reading the people pledge obedience to Joshua, and in Romans Paul warns against judging others while God's kindness waits. Jesus in Matthew asks for the love that refuses to repay. The two main readings belong together: a person who carries God's image does not answer evil with evil, and neither does the God whose image it is. The key words are image, breath and the second mile.

set: The poem of seven days reaches its summit on the sixth day and its rest on the seventh. Then, at 2:4, a second account begins, older in style according to many scholars and more homely, where God works with his hands like a potter. The two were set side by side, and each says what the other leaves out: humanity's dignity at the top of creation, and humanity's closeness to the soil.
str: 1:20–23: day five: the waters and the sky fill.
1:24–31: day six: animals, then humankind, male and female.
2:1–3: the seventh day: God rests and hallows it.
2:4–7: a new beginning: dust and breath.
kw: In the ancient East a king was “the image” of a god, and his statues stood for him in distant provinces. Genesis gives this title to every man and woman, not to a king alone.
A Hebrew play on words: the human is named from the soil. ’Ādām in 1:26–27 means humankind, “male and female”, not one male.
The same words are used of the animals in 1:24. What is distinctive in 2:7 is the way life comes: God breathes it in.
vv: Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness;
Many scholars hear in “us” a plural of solemn deliberation, or God addressing his heavenly court. Many Fathers, reading with the New Testament, heard a first hint of the Trinity.
So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
The verb bārā’ comes three times in a single verse. Man and woman alike bear the image. No human being, however poor, sick or despised, stands outside this verse.
God saw everything that he had made, and indeed, it was very good.
For the first time the refrain says “very”. The body is part of what is called very good. Christian fasting begins from this verse and never contradicts it.
then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and the man became a living being.

The word for “formed” is the potter's word (compare Isaiah 45:9). Dust and breath lie together in one sentence. Jesus repeats the gesture when he breathes on his disciples on Easter evening (John 20:22), and Paul contrasts Adam with “the last Adam”, a “life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45).
ch: The Catechism teaches that being in God's image gives every person the dignity of being someone, not something (CCC 357), and that the human being is one, at once bodily and spiritual (CCC 362). It says that “subduing” the earth is the vocation of stewards (CCC 373), as Pope Francis insists in Laudato Si' (67). It also quotes St Irenaeus, who says that God fashioned man with his own two hands, the Son and the Spirit (CCC 704).

set: This is the fifth of the six contrasts in the Sermon on the Mount. The law's “eye for an eye” (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20) was not a licence for revenge. In its day it limited revenge: only one eye for one eye, and in the hands of a judge, not a feud. Jesus goes further and asks his disciples to give up the claim altogether.
str: v. 38: the old rule of measure.
v. 39a: the principle.
vv. 39b–41: three examples: the insult, the lawsuit, forced service.
v. 42: generosity to the one who asks.
kw: To stand against, to oppose. The sense here is: do not pay back in the same coin.
The inner garment and the outer one. The law protected a poor person's cloak, which was to be returned by nightfall (Exodus 22:26–27).
A loanword from Persian. An official or soldier could requisition a local person to carry a load. Matthew uses the same verb for Simon of Cyrene (27:32).
vv: But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also;

Many scholars note that a right-handed blow to the right cheek would be with the back of the hand, an insult more than an attack. The answer Jesus asks for is neither to strike back nor to shrink into hatred.
and if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.
The first mile is compelled. The second is a gift, and it changes what the whole journey means: the disciple is no longer merely a victim, but someone who serves.
Give to everyone who begs from you,
Almsgiving belongs with the Fast. The sentence does not settle every practical question of how best to help; it does close the heart's excuses.
ch: This teaching does not take away the duty of protecting the weak. The Church teaches that legitimate defence can even be a grave duty for those responsible for others (CCC 2263–2265), and that Jesus' teaching rules out anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262). Jesus himself, when struck, asked, “why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). St Augustine draws from this that the command concerns the readiness of the heart, not only the outward gesture (in substance). The summit of this teaching is the Cross.

qa: Is the Christian bound to accept abuse in silence?

No. Jesus speaks of renouncing revenge, not of leaving the innocent unprotected. A person suffering violence at home, for example, may and should seek safety and help. Forgiving does not mean giving up the truth or justice.
study: When was I last tempted to pay someone back? What would the “second mile” have looked like?
How does it change my way of seeing someone I dislike to recall that he or she carries God's image and breath?

lead: Today's first reading says that a person is made for another: “It is not good that the man should be alone”. The reading from Joshua tells of Rahab, the foreign woman who protects the spies, and Paul in Romans says that hearing the law is not enough without doing it. Matthew turns to prayer, which is the deepest relationship of all, and asks that it be real: before the Father, not before an audience. The first reading speaks of being unashamed before one another, and the Gospel of being unpretending before God. The key words are helper, one flesh and in secret.

set: In this second account of creation, the man is formed first, placed in the garden, and given his task. Then, for the first time in the Bible, something is “not good”, and it is not sin. It is loneliness. The scene that follows is told like a story for children, with a gentle humour, and it carries one of the deepest teachings of Scripture on marriage.
str: v. 18: God's verdict and God's plan.
vv. 19–20: the animals are named, and none is the right partner.
vv. 21–22: deep sleep, the rib, the woman brought to the man.
v. 23: the first human song.
vv. 24–25: the narrator's conclusion: one flesh, and no shame.
kw: ‘Ēzer does not mean a servant: it is often used of God himself, as in Psalm 121:2. Kənegdô means “corresponding to him”, one who stands face to face with him.
The word usually means a side, as of the ark or the tabernacle in Exodus. She comes from his side, neither above nor below him.
A Hebrew play on sounds which the NRSV keeps with “Man” and “Woman”. The POC's “നരൻ / നാരി” catches it beautifully.
vv: Then the Lord God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper as his partner.”

After the seven-fold “good” of chapter 1, this “not good” is a surprise. It teaches that we are made for communion: human beings are not complete alone. This does not diminish the single life, which also knows communion with God and others.
This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh;
“At last”: the man has seen every creature and found no partner. Now he breaks into song. Woman and man recognise each other as equals, of one nature.
Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.

Jesus quotes this verse when he answers the question on divorce and adds that what God has joined, no one is to separate (Matthew 19:5–6). The Letter to the Ephesians applies it to Christ and the Church: “a great mystery” (5:31–32).
And the man and his wife were both naked, and were not ashamed.
They have nothing to hide from each other or from God. The Hebrew word for “naked” (‘ārûmmîm) sounds like the word for “crafty” (‘ārûm) in the very next verse, 3:1, where the serpent enters.
ch: The Catechism teaches that man and woman were created in perfect equality as persons, and for each other (CCC 369–372), and that this page is the foundation of its teaching on marriage (CCC 1601–1605). The Fathers saw in the man's deep sleep a figure of Christ on the Cross. The Catechism, quoting St Ambrose, says: as Eve was formed from the sleeping Adam's side, so the Church was born from the pierced heart of Christ (CCC 766). At every Holy Qurbana we draw near to that side.

set: Matthew 6:1–18 takes three practices of Jewish piety which Jesus and his disciples kept: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. They are precisely the three works of the Great Fast. Jesus keeps all three, and asks only about the motive: for whose eyes? Today's reading deals with prayer.
str: v. 5: do not pray to be seen.
v. 6: go in, shut the door, pray to your Father.
vv. 7–8: do not multiply words; your Father knows.
kw: In Greek, the word for a stage actor. Prayer as a performance has an audience, and the audience's applause is all the reward it receives.
An inner room or storeroom, perhaps the only room in a poor house with a door that closed.
A rare word found only here in the New Testament, perhaps imitating the sound of babbling.
vv: And whenever you pray, do not be like the hypocrites;

Standing was the normal posture of Jewish prayer, and synagogue and street were not wrong places for it. Jesus himself prayed in public. The warning is against a fault found among religious people of every age, including Christians: prayer that looks round to see who is watching.
But whenever you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret;

This does not cancel the Church's common prayer; Jesus goes on to teach “Our Father”, in the plural. He teaches where prayer starts: in a heart alone with God. The Father is “in secret”, and he is found there.
Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
Then why ask? Because prayer is not information for God. It is a child's trust, and it changes the one who prays.
ch: The Catechism counts prayer to the Father in secret, and not heaping up empty phrases, among the conversions of heart that Jesus asks of those who pray (CCC 2608). In the Syriac tradition, Aphrahat, the Persian Sage, in his treatise on prayer, says that the room is the heart, and the door to be shut is the mouth (in substance). This is the school of the Fast.

qa: Does Genesis 2 make woman inferior, because she comes second and from his rib?
No. The story's point is the opposite: none of the animals is his equal, and she alone is. The Church teaches their equal dignity as persons (CCC 369). Later abuse of this text was never its meaning.
study: Where do I find it hardest to be without a mask: before God, in my marriage or family, or among friends?
What would one “shut door” each day of the Fast look like in my house?

lead: Genesis tells how trust was lost: a serpent's question, a fruit, fig leaves, and God's voice asking, “Where are you?” In the second reading God promises Joshua, “I will be with you”, and in Romans Paul concludes that all alike are under sin. Matthew offers the cure of that first distrust: look at the birds and lilies, and rely on a Father who knows. The first sin began by doubting God's goodness; the Gospel of today teaches a child's trust in it. The key words are crafty, where are you and worry.

set: After the peace of chapter 2, the story turns. The man and woman live in the garden with one command: “of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (2:17). The story is told with the simple depth of a parable, and any reader recognises the steps of temptation from the inside. The reading stops at 3:13, before God's sentence and his first promise in 3:15.
str: vv. 1–5: the serpent's conversation.
v. 6: the fruit is seen, taken, eaten and shared.
v. 7: open eyes, and shame.
vv. 8–10: they hide, and God calls.
vv. 11–13: the questions, and the blame passed along.
kw: The same sound as “naked” in 2:25. The couple were unashamed; the serpent is clever, and his cleverness will leave them naked in a new way.
The text calls it a creature of God, not a rival god. The Book of Wisdom sees behind it “the devil's envy” (2:24), and Revelation 12:9 names the ancient serpent.
One word in Hebrew. God asks not because he lacks knowledge but in order to call. It is the first question God puts to a human being in the Bible.
vv: Did God say, ‘You shall not eat from any tree in the garden’?

The serpent begins with a distortion. God had given every tree but one. The question makes the generous God look like a miser. Note that the woman's answer adds “nor shall you touch it” (3:3), which the command in 2:17 did not say. The conversation has already blurred what God said.
for God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.
Here is the heart of the lie: God is holding something back from you. To be like God is in fact their dignity already (1:27). The temptation is to seize it apart from him.
So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes,
Sin arrives through ordinary goods: food, beauty, wisdom. Last Sunday's Gospel (Matthew 4:1–11) showed Jesus refusing the same kind of temptations, in the desert, while fasting.
But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
Before any penalty there is a search. The whole Bible could be read as the story of this question, carried on until the Good Shepherd goes after the lost.
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”
He blames the woman and, in the same breath, God (“whom you gave”). She blames the serpent. The “one flesh” of yesterday's reading has become mutual accusation.
ch: The Catechism says that the account uses figurative language but affirms a primeval event, at the beginning of human history (CCC 390). Man, tempted by the devil, let his trust in his Creator die in his heart (CCC 397); harmony was then lost (CCC 399–400). But God did not abandon him (CCC 410). St Basil, preaching on fasting, points out that the first command in Paradise was a command to fast, “you shall not eat”, and that our loss began there (in substance). So the fast is a road back.

set: The “Therefore” links these verses to 6:24: “You cannot serve God and wealth.” Anxiety about tomorrow is one form of serving wealth. Jesus speaks to ordinary people in Galilee, who may really wonder about food and clothing. He does not say that these needs are unreal, but he does say who knows about them.
str: v. 25: do not worry about life and body.
vv. 26–27: the birds; worry adds nothing.
vv. 28–30: the lilies and the grass.
vv. 31–32: your Father knows.
v. 33: strive first for the kingdom.
v. 34: one day at a time.
kw: It is the key verb, six times in these ten verses. It means an anxiety that pulls the mind apart, not sensible planning.
Almost a word of Matthew's own, used gently to the disciples (see 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). They have faith, but it is small.
God's reign and God's right order for life. They give the priority by which everything else finds its place.
vv: Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
It is not a lesson in laziness: birds work hard for their food, and Paul demands that Christians work too. The point is the Father. Jesus' argument runs: how much more you.
And can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?
The Greek means either a cubit added to one's height or a small length added to one's life. The POC keeps the measure, “മുഴം”; the NRSV turns it into time. In either case, worry adds nothing.
But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
This verse is the centre. It does not say that bread is unimportant. It says what comes first. Those who hold back from food in the Fast are saying the same with their bodies.
Today’s trouble is enough for today.
A piece of practical wisdom, with a smile in it. Grace is given for today, like the manna, not for imagined tomorrows.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when teaching that Jesus asks for childlike abandonment to the providence of our heavenly Father (CCC 305), and it links “strive first” with the petition for daily bread (CCC 2830). Trust does not exempt anyone from work or from the care of the poor. In the Father's plan those who have more are often the means by which he feeds those who have less.

qa: Was the fruit an apple, and must the story be taken word for word?

The text says only “fruit”. The apple probably comes from later Western art, and many suggest a play on the Latin malum, which can mean both “apple” and “evil”. As for the story, the Church says that its language is figurative but that it affirms a real event at the beginning of human history (CCC 390).
study: What lie about God do I find easiest to believe when I am tempted?
What am I anxious about today? What would “strive first” mean in that matter?

lead: The sin that began as distrust of God now becomes violence against a brother. Genesis tells of Cain and Abel. The second reading shows Israel crossing the Jordan and setting up stones, and Paul in Romans holds up the faith of Abraham. In Matthew, Jesus warns against judging and asks us to attend first to the log in our own eye. Cain is angry about his brother's standing with God; the Gospel removes the grounds for that kind of comparison. The key words are brother, lurking and measure.

set: This is the first story outside the garden and the first in the Bible about brothers. In one generation, sin has moved from eating a forbidden fruit to murder. It is also a story of ways of life, the farmer and the shepherd, and it does not explain everything: the reason why God accepts one offering and not the other is left unstated.
str: vv. 1–2: two births.
vv. 3–5: two offerings, and Cain's anger.
vv. 6–7: God warns Cain.
v. 8: the murder.
vv. 9–12: the question, the blood, the sentence.
vv. 13–16: Cain's cry, God's protective mark, and the departure.
kw: Eve's word sounds like her son's name. It is a word of joy, and she credits the Lord.
The name means breath or vapour, the same word as “vanity” in Ecclesiastes. Abel never speaks in the story, and he passes like breath.
A word for an animal crouching. Sin waits at the door like a beast. The Hebrew word for “desire” here also comes in 3:16.
vv: If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is lurking at the door; its desire is for you, but you must master it.

God speaks to Cain before the crime, as a father to a son. Anger is not yet murder, and Cain is still able to choose. The Hebrew of this verse is hard, but its sense is clear: no one is forced to sin.
Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let us go out to the field.”

A note on the text. The standard Hebrew text has “Cain said to his brother Abel” with no words following. The Greek, Syriac and other ancient versions supply “Let us go out to the field”, and the NRSV and POC follow them. Once they are in the field, the word “brother” keeps sounding, seven times in the passage: this is what is being killed.
He said, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?”
God again asks a question, as in the garden. Cain answers with a lie and then with a sneer. The whole Bible answers yes.
Listen; your brother’s blood is crying out to me from the ground!
The one who never spoke is heard after all. God hears the cry of those no one defends. Hebrews says that the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (12:24): it asks for mercy.
And the Lord put a mark on Cain, so that no one who came upon him would kill him.
The mark is not a brand of shame, as people often think. It is a sign of protection, and God keeps the murderer alive.
ch: The Catechism says that this account reveals the presence of anger and envy in man from the beginning of history (CCC 2259), and it counts the blood of Abel among the sins that cry out to heaven (CCC 1867). St John Paul II gave a long meditation on the passage in Evangelium Vitae (7–10), and wrote that not even a murderer loses his personal dignity, which God himself pledges to guarantee (9). Why was Cain's offering refused? Hebrews says that Abel offered “by faith” (11:4), and 1 John that Cain's “own deeds were evil” (3:12).

r.h: The log in your own eye
set: Near the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns to the way disciples treat one another. They have just heard about prayer and trust. Now he warns them against the temptation of religious people everywhere: to use their progress as a measuring rod for others.
str: vv. 1–2: do not judge; the measure returns.
vv. 3–5: the speck and the log.
v. 6: what is holy, and the dogs and swine.
kw: It can mean to discern or to condemn. Here it means the second: taking God's seat over another person.
A chip of straw and a roof-beam. It is a joke from a carpenter's workshop, and his hearers surely smiled.
The measure used in the market for grain. “Measure for measure” was also a known saying of Jewish teachers (Mishnah, Sotah 1:7).
vv: Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.

The passive means: by God. This is the sense of the warning: do not stand where God alone stands. It does not forbid telling right from wrong, for later in this chapter Jesus asks his disciples to recognise false prophets by their fruits (7:15–16), and in 18:15 he speaks of correcting a brother.
You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor’s eye.
He does not forbid helping with the speck. He gives the order. One who has known the pain of the log will be gentle with another's eye.
Do not give what is holy to dogs; and do not throw your pearls before swine,

A hard proverb whose meaning is not certain. It is not a description of any people. It asks for reverence in handing on what is holy, and so balances vv. 1–5. The Didache (9:5) applied it to the Eucharist: only the baptised are to receive it.
ch: The Catechism names rash judgment as a sin against truth and asks us to interpret others' words and deeds as favourably as we can, quoting St Ignatius of Loyola (CCC 2477–2478). The Fast is a good time for this: the Church gives us the Sacrament of Reconciliation, where each person speaks only of the log in his or her own eye.

qa: Why did God prefer Abel's offering? Isn't that unfair?

The text does not say why, and this silence is deliberate. It notes that Abel brought the “firstlings” and “fat portions”, the best, and it says of Cain only “the fruit of the ground”. The New Testament sees the difference in the heart (Hebrews 11:4; 1 John 3:12). The story's question is what Cain does when he feels passed over, and that is a question for all of us.
study: Whom do I secretly compare myself with? How does that show in my words about that person?
Name a “log” in your own eye that you could bring to Confession during this Fast.

lead: On Saturday there are two readings, and they meet at one point: forgiveness. Paul in Romans, after showing on Thursday that all are under sin, now opens the door: God justifies by his grace as a gift. Jesus in Matthew gives the prayer of those who live by that gift, and adds that the forgiven must forgive. At the end of the first week of the Fast they remind us that the Fast does not buy God's favour; it answers it. The key words are grace, Father and debts.

set: Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, a Church he did not found, probably from Corinth about AD 57 or 58. Since 1:18 he has been showing that Gentile and Jew alike stand in need of God's mercy, and that section ended with every mouth silenced (3:19). These six verses are the turning point of the letter. Many scholars count them among the most packed sentences Paul wrote.
str: v. 21: “But now”: God's righteousness is shown, apart from law, and attested by law and prophets.
v. 22: through faith, for all.
vv. 23–24: all have sinned; all are justified as a gift.
vv. 25–26: the Cross shows God's righteousness and forbearance.
kw: Not only a quality God has, but what he does: he keeps faith and puts people right with himself.
The word for buying a captive or slave back. In Scripture it recalls the Exodus.

In the Greek Old Testament this is the “mercy seat”, the lid of the ark, sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14; compare Hebrews 9:5). Paul places Christ where that meeting between God and his people took place.
vv: But now, apart from law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, and is attested by the law and the prophets,

“But now” is one of the great turns in Scripture. Note what Paul holds together: it comes “apart from law”, yet the law itself bears witness. He is not setting Israel's Scriptures aside. He reads them as a promise.
the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.

A note on the text. The Greek phrase can be read “faith in Jesus Christ” or “the faith of Jesus Christ”, that is, his own faithfulness; the NRSV notes this in its margin. Scholars still discuss it. Either way, the source of salvation is Christ, and our part is to believe.
since all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God;
“All” is the point: Paul has no one in mind to look down on. Many read this “glory” as what Adam's race was meant to carry, the likeness of God that Tuesday's reading spoke of.
they are now justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
“As a gift” (dōrean) and “by his grace” say the same thing twice. Nobody pays for this.
ch: The Catechism quotes this very passage to say that justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ (CCC 1992), and it teaches that grace comes first, while good works done in grace are themselves God's gift and bear fruit (CCC 1996; 2006–2011). The Council of Trent taught that nothing before justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification (Session 6, chapter 8). In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans declared together: “By grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part”, we are accepted by God (Joint Declaration, 15).

set: The prayer stands near the centre of the Sermon on the Mount, immediately after the warning against many words. Luke gives a shorter form (11:2–4). Matthew's form is the one the Church's worship has prayed from early times. The Didache (8:2–3) tells Christians to say it three times a day. Each petition has roots in the prayers of Israel; calling God Father was known in Israel, and it is the mark of Jesus' own prayer.
str: v. 9a: the address.
vv. 9b–10: three petitions for God: name, kingdom, will.
vv. 11–13: three (or four) for us: bread, forgiveness, trial, rescue.
vv. 14–15: Jesus' own comment on forgiveness.
kw: A rare word, whose meaning was already debated by Origen. It may mean “for today”, “for tomorrow” or “needed for life”, and St Jerome's Latin in Matthew has “supersubstantial”. The Catechism keeps both the plain bread and the Eucharist in view (CCC 2837).
Sin as a debt owed. In Aramaic the same word serves for debt and for sin, and Luke (11:4) writes “sins”.
It means both testing and temptation. The Catechism explains the petition as asking not to enter into temptation or be overcome by it (CCC 2846). God tempts no one.
vv: Pray then in this way: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.
“Our”: even in the shut room we pray in the plural. God's name is made holy first by God, and then in the lives of those who bear it.
Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
In Gethsemane Jesus will pray in the same words (26:42). This is not resignation. It asks that earth become as obedient as heaven.
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

The only petition with a condition, and the only one on which Jesus comments (vv. 14–15). God's mercy is never earned, but a closed heart cannot receive it (CCC 2840). This takes up the reconciliation of Monday's Gospel.
but if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

A hard word in a hard case: forgiving does not always mean feeling peaceful or forgetting. The Catechism says that it is not in our power not to feel or forget an offence, but the heart that offers itself to the Spirit turns injury into compassion (CCC 2843).
ch: Tertullian calls this prayer the summary of the whole Gospel, as the Catechism recalls (CCC 2761), and St Augustine says that all other prayers of Scripture are contained in it (in substance; CCC 2762). The last petition asks for rescue from “the evil one”, and the Catechism says that evil here is no abstraction but a person, Satan (CCC 2851).

qa: If grace is a gift, why do we fast at all?

Because a gift is received with a life. We do not fast in order to make God love us. We fast because he loves us, and because the body and heart need clearing to receive what he gives. Paul himself speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Merit in Catholic teaching is itself the work of grace (CCC 2008).
rite: The Holy Qurbana of the East Syriac tradition opens with the Lord's Prayer and prays it again before Communion. In its liturgical form the Syro-Malabar Church prays “our debts and our sins”, keeping both senses of the word.
study: Which line of the Our Father do I find hardest to mean today, and why?
Paul says “But now”. Where have I seen God's “but now” in my own life?

lead: On this Second Sunday of the Great Fast the readings ask what a life stands on. Genesis lists long lives that all end the same way, with one name that breaks the pattern: “Enoch walked with God”. In Joshua, Israel comes up out of the Jordan and sets up stones so that children will ask what they mean. Paul tells those who crossed the waters of baptism that everyone serves someone, and that sin pays in death but God gives life as a gift. Jesus closes the Sermon on the Mount with two houses and one storm. The line runs from walking, to crossing, to serving, to building, and its key words are walked, remember, gift and rock.

set: Chapter 5 is a genealogy, running in ten generations from Adam to Noah through Seth. Israel's neighbours also had lists from before the flood: the Sumerian King List gives reigns of enormous length. In Genesis the list has a rhythm: so-and-so lived, had children, and “he died”. It is a sermon on what sin brought, and on the fact that God's blessing to “be fruitful” continues through it. The numbers differ in the Hebrew, Samaritan and Greek texts, so they should not be pressed as a plain record.
str: vv. 19–20: Jared, nine hundred sixty-two years; “and he died”.
vv. 21–24: Enoch, the seventh from Adam (Jude 14), and no “he died”.
vv. 25–27: Methuselah, the longest of all, and “he died”.
vv. 28–31: Lamech, and the naming of Noah.
¶ The refrain makes Enoch stand out. His three hundred sixty-five years also match the days of the solar year, and many commentators think this is no accident: a complete life.
kw: The verb means to walk to and fro, habitually. It is used again of Noah (6:9). The Greek Old Testament reads “pleased God”, which Sirach 44:16 and Hebrews 11:5 echo, and the POC's “ദൈവത്തിനു പ്രിയങ്കരനായി” stands close to that sense.
An ordinary verb for “take”, used again of Elijah, whom the Lord would take away (2 Kings 2:3). The text does not explain where Enoch went.
Lamech's saying (v. 29) plays on a Hebrew verb for comfort or relief. A name becomes a prayer.
vv: Thus all the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty-two years; and he died.
The refrain is a bell. It carries out the word of 3:19, “to dust you shall return”, which was spoken over us on Vibhoodi. Great age does not change the last word.
Enoch walked with God after the birth of Methuselah three hundred years, and had other sons and daughters.
Enoch's holiness is lived at home among children. Nothing here speaks of a desert or a cave. The same is offered to a father and mother in a Kerala house during the Fast.
Enoch walked with God; then he was no more, because God took him.

The verse leaves the mystery alone. Later Jewish writers built a large literature around Enoch, and Jude 14–15 quotes from one such book. What matters is the first half of the sentence. Walking comes before being taken.
he named him Noah, saying, “Out of the ground that the Lord has cursed this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the toil of our hands.”
These are the only spoken words in the chapter. A tired father looks at his son and hopes. The curse of 3:17 is remembered, and hope for relief runs ahead toward one who is greater than Noah.
ch: Sirach calls Enoch “an example of repentance to all generations” (44:16), which is why he suits this season so well. Hebrews places him in its list of faith: “he had pleased God” (11:5). St Irenaeus notes that Enoch pleased God without circumcision (in substance): the friendship of God is older than any sign. The Fast is a return to that first thing: to walk with God, step by step, in the house where we live.

set: After Moses' death Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan into the land. Chapters 3–4 tell the crossing as a liturgy more than a military campaign: priests carry the ark into the river, the waters stand still, the people cross, and twelve stones are taken from the riverbed. Many scholars think that the book reached its form long after the events, and that Israel's own later worship at Gilgal lies behind this telling. The reading is the close of the crossing.
str: vv. 15–18: at God's word the priests come up, and the river returns.
v. 19: the date and the camp at Gilgal.
vv. 20–22: the stones and the children's question.
vv. 23–24: Jordan and Red Sea together; the purpose: all peoples, and fear of the Lord.
kw: The sign of God's presence with his word. The waters stay back as long as it stands in the river: the crossing is God's doing.
The name is usually linked with a word for circle or rolling, and is often explained as a circle of stones. Here Israel will also keep the Passover (5:10).
The word of Genesis 1:9, “let the dry land appear”, and of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:16). The God who made the land appear at creation makes it appear again for his people.
vv: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month,
This is the date when the Passover lamb was to be chosen (Exodus 12:3). The new life in the land begins with a Passover calendar.
When your children ask their parents in time to come, ‘What do these stones mean?’

Israel teaches by provoking a child's question, as at the Passover (Exodus 12:26). The stones do not speak by themselves; parents have to tell the story. That is what families do when a child asks why there is no meat this week.
For the Lord your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you crossed over, as the Lord your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we crossed over,

“For you... for us”: the speaker merges the generations. Those who crossed the Red Sea are mostly dead, yet the story is “ours”. This is how Scripture remembers, and how the Church does in the Holy Qurbana.
so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the Lord is mighty,
The miracle is not for Israel's pride. God's acts are meant to be seen by all peoples. So the reading looks beyond any one nation.
ch: The Catechism says that the crossing of the Jordan, by which God's people received the land, is an image of eternal life, and it is among the figures of Baptism (CCC 1222). Origen, in his homilies on Joshua, reads the crossing as a figure of Baptism (in substance). In the Greek Bible, Joshua's name is the same as the name of Jesus, and the Fathers made much of it: Jesus leads us through the water into the promise. The Great Fast was the ancient time when catechumens prepared for Baptism at Easter, so these verses speak directly to the season.

set: Paul has just said that “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (5:20). He knows how this will be heard: then let us go on sinning. He answers that objection at 6:1 with Baptism, “buried with him” (6:4), and answers it here again at v. 15 with the image of slavery. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, and some of his hearers in Rome were likely slaves themselves. The image is meant to be startling.
str: v. 15: the objection.
v. 16: everyone serves someone.
vv. 17–18: you were slaves of sin; thanks be to God.
v. 19: Paul apologises for his human image; he asks for your members.
vv. 20–22: compare the two harvests.
v. 23: wages and gift.
kw: The word Paul uses of himself in 1:1. There is no neutral, unowned human life: the choice is whom to obey.
Many scholars think that this refers to the instruction given before Baptism. The Christian is “handed over” to the teaching, as a metal is to a mould.
Opsōnia was a term for a soldier's pay. Charisma is a gift of grace. Sin pays what it owes, while God gives what nobody earned (even our merit comes from his grace: CCC 2008).
Holiness as a process and a harvest. It is the fruit that grows in those belonging to God (vv. 19, 22).
vv: What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!
Grace does not loosen the moral life; it makes it possible. To be “under grace” does not mean that nothing matters. It means that for the first time we are able to obey.
But thanks be to God that you, having once been slaves of sin, have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were entrusted,
“From the heart” is the point. The Fast is a time of outward works, and Paul shows what they are for. Inner obedience is a thing to thank God for, because it is his work.
I am speaking in human terms because of your natural limitations.
Paul knows that the image limps. God is no slave-driver. He uses the image in order to say that belonging is total.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

This verse is a gift to preachers. St Augustine noticed its surprise: Paul could have said that the wages of righteousness is eternal life, but he chose to say that it is a gift (in substance). We earn death. We can only be given life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that there is no true liberty except in the service of what is good and just, and that the choice to disobey is an abuse of liberty that leads to the slavery of sin (CCC 1733). On death as the consequence of sin, see CCC 1008. This is why the Church places the works of the Fast beside Baptism: each act of penance is a small daily return to what happened at the font. At every Holy Qurbana we receive the gift that verse 23 names.

set: These are the last words of the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), and Matthew then says the crowds were astounded (7:28). The closing warning is addressed to people who already know Jesus and call him Lord, and it applies especially to the religious.
str: v. 21: not saying, but doing.
vv. 22–23: “On that day”: great deeds, and “I never knew you”.
vv. 24–25: the wise builder.
vv. 26–27: the foolish builder.
¶ The two houses are the same in everything: same words heard, same rain, same wind. The foundation alone differs, and it cannot be seen until the storm.
kw: The doubled address is respectful and earnest. The title itself is right, and Jesus does not reject it. It simply is not enough.
Literally “you who work lawlessness”. The words echo Psalm 6:8. In Matthew the failure is to neglect the will of the Father.
The same pair as the ten bridesmaids (25:1–13). In Matthew, wisdom means hearing Jesus' word and doing it.
vv: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.

Jesus is the judge in this sentence, and this is an astonishing claim from a teacher on a hillside. “My Father” occurs here for the first time on his lips in Matthew's Gospel, and doing the Father's will is what he himself will pray for in Gethsemane.
Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; go away from me, you evildoers.’
Their gifts may have been real. Prophecy and miracles can be done in Jesus' name by those who do not love him. To “know” here means the relationship of the covenant, and that is what they lack.
Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
“These words of mine”: the whole Sermon. Jesus places his own teaching as the foundation, where Israel's teachers would place God's law. It is a claim about who he is.
The rain fell, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall,

In the dry valleys of Palestine a winter storm can send a sudden torrent through a place that looked safe. Readers in Kerala need no explanation. The wise man is not spared the storm. Both houses take the same rain.
ch: The Catechism says that the prayer of faith consists not only in saying “Lord, Lord”, but in disposing the heart to do the Father's will (CCC 2611), and that the New Law demands a decisive choice between “the two ways”, to put the Lord's words into practice (CCC 1970). The Second Vatican Council warns that a person who remains in the Church in body but does not persevere in charity is not saved (Lumen Gentium 14). As St James says, “be doers of the word” (1:22). St Augustine reads the rock as Christ himself (in substance), as Paul does in 1 Corinthians 10:4.

qa: How could people live for nine hundred years?

Genesis is not giving a medical record. Other peoples of the ancient East recorded vast ages before the flood, and the numbers differ among the ancient copies of Genesis itself. The Church does not require us to count them as modern statistics. Their teaching lies elsewhere: in the blessing that continues, in the death that comes to all, and in the one who walked with God.
Did Enoch go to heaven before Christ?

The text says only that “God took him”, and Hebrews 11:5 says that he “did not experience death”. Scripture does not say where he went, and the Church has defined nothing on it. What the New Testament does say is that “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3:13), and the Catechism teaches that Christ alone opens that way to us (CCC 661).
Paul says that we are saved by gift, and Jesus says we must do the will of the Father. Do they disagree?

No. Both speak of one life. Paul says that the source is grace, and he insists in today's epistle that those who receive it become obedient “from the heart”. Jesus speaks of the fruit by which that life is known. The Church holds them together as “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6; see CCC 1814–1816).
rite: This is the Second Sunday of the Great Fast, the Sauma Ramba. Through the first week the calendar has read Genesis and Joshua together with Romans and the Sermon on the Mount, and Genesis has moved from creation to the line of Seth. In the Syriac tradition, Aphrahat the Persian Sage taught in his treatise on fasting that a pure heart is a better fast than abstaining from bread and water alone (in substance). The Fast is the digging of a foundation: this is what the ash, the abstinence and the Friday Way of the Cross are for. As the stones at Gilgal do, these customs prompt children to ask, and we are to tell them.
study: Enoch walked with God while raising a family. Which ordinary part of my day could become a place of walking with God?
What are the “stones” in our home and parish that make children ask? Do we tell them the story?
Paul says that everyone serves someone. Looking at how I actually spend my time and money, whom do I serve?
If a storm came this week, what would my house be found to be standing on? What one thing from the Sermon on the Mount will I act on in this Fast?

lead: The second week of the Great Fast opens with the question of what really makes a person clean. Titus recalls what Christians once were and what God's mercy did for them, “through the water of rebirth”. In Mark, Jesus teaches that defilement comes “from the human heart”, and not from the plate. Together they explain why we fast: food cannot stain us, but a heart washed by God can learn to live differently. The key words are mercy, washing and within.

r.h: Not because of our works, but according to his mercy
set: Titus was a Gentile co-worker of Paul (Galatians 2:3), and this letter places him on the island of Crete, where he is to put the young churches in order (1:5). With 1 and 2 Timothy it forms the group called the Pastoral Letters. The letter bears Paul's name. Many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name after his death, while others hold that Paul wrote it through a secretary. The Church receives it as inspired Scripture in either case. The Christians it addresses are a small group living among neighbours who watch how they behave.
str: vv. 1–2: how to live in public: respect for authority, readiness for good work, gentleness toward everyone.
v. 3: what we ourselves once were.
vv. 4–7: what God did: mercy, washing, the Spirit, the hope of eternal life.
¶ Many scholars think vv. 4–7 echo an early baptismal formula or hymn, since the next verse says, “The saying is sure” (3:8).
kw: Literally love for human beings; our word “philanthropy” comes from it. Greek writers praised this virtue in kings. Here it belongs to God our Savior.
Literally the “washing of rebirth”. The word palingenesia occurs only one other time in the New Testament, at Matthew 19:28.
In v. 2 this is said of speech about any person, and it is the same family of words as “slander” in Mark 7:22.
vv: to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show every courtesy to everyone.
“No one” stands at one end of this verse and “everyone” at the other. Christian manners are not kept for fellow Christians.
For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray,
The writer counts himself in. Nobody can despise a neighbour after honestly remembering his own past.
he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
This is the heart of the passage. Our fast does not buy God's mercy; the mercy came first and it reached us at the font.
ch: The Catechism takes this verse as one of the names of Baptism: it is the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, because it signifies and brings about birth of water and the Spirit (CCC 1215). Good works are not set aside, since v. 1 asks for them and v. 8 returns to them. They grow from grace and do not earn the first grace (CCC 2010).

r.h: From within, from the human heart
set: Pharisees and scribes have asked why Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands (7:1–5). The purity rules were a holy thing for observant Jews, a way of living every day as a people set apart for God. Jesus has answered sharply about human custom set above God's command (7:6–13). Now he turns to the crowd and goes to the root of the matter. Mark explains Jewish customs for his readers (7:3–4), so he is probably writing for many who were Gentiles, to whom this question of food mattered greatly.
str: vv. 14–15: the short saying to the crowd.
vv. 17–19: in the house, the disciples ask, and food is explained.
vv. 20–23: what comes out: a list of evils from the heart.
¶ A note on the text. The NRSV has no v. 16, because the oldest manuscripts lack it. The Malayalam POC keeps it, a call to anyone with ears to hear (compare 4:23).
kw: Literally “to make common”, the opposite of set apart for God. The word runs through the whole passage.
In the Bible the heart is less the seat of feeling than the centre of the person, where one thinks, decides and chooses.
Literally “an evil eye”, one of the twelve items in the list. It looks at another's good and wishes it were not so.
vv: there is nothing outside a person that by going in can defile, but the things that come out are what defile.
Jesus does not despise the Law, which itself asks for a clean heart (Psalm 51:10). He names what the Law's outward signs were always pointing to.
(Thus he declared all foods clean.)
This is Mark's own comment. The early Church needed time to work out its meaning for table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers (Acts 10:15; Acts 15; Galatians 2:11–14).
For it is from within, from the human heart, that evil intentions come:
Evil intentions come first and the deeds follow. In Greek, six plural words (fornication to wickedness) are followed by six singular ones (deceit to folly).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus here perfects the dietary law by revealing its teaching purpose (CCC 582). It cites the same sayings to show that the root of sin lies in the heart (CCC 1853), and that the heart is the seat of moral personality (CCC 2517). Respect for the people of the Law belongs to any honest reading of this passage (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).

qa: If all foods are clean, why do we abstain in the Great Fast?

We do not abstain because meat is unclean. Fasting is a chosen discipline: it teaches the body to say no, makes room for prayer, and gives us something to share with the poor. It is one of the ways interior penance is expressed (CCC 1434, 1438).
study: Which item in Mark's list do I most need to bring to the Lord during this fast?
Titus 3:2 asks us to speak evil of no one. What would a fast of the tongue look like in my home this week?

lead: Both readings teach us to ask and to wait. Paul hears the whole of creation groaning like a woman in labour, and says that we groan with it while we wait in hope. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his disciples to keep asking, seeking and knocking, because the one they ask is their Father. The fast is a season for this kind of longing. The key words are hope, groaning and ask.

set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome around AD 57, probably from Corinth, to a church he had not yet visited. Romans 8 is the high point of the letter's first part. It describes life in the Spirit: we are children of God and heirs with Christ, “if, in fact, we suffer with him” (8:17). Our passage takes up that suffering, and sets it against what is to come.
str: v. 18: the thesis: present suffering against coming glory.
vv. 19–22: creation waits, subjected to futility, groaning in labour.
vv. 23–25: we also groan, and we hope for what we do not see.
kw: A rare word, found in the New Testament only here and at Philippians 1:20. It suggests someone craning the neck to see what is coming.
The word the Greek Old Testament uses for “vanity” in Ecclesiastes. Creation cannot reach its goal; it is like a work left unfinished.
The first part of the harvest, which is a pledge of the rest. The Spirit we already have is the beginning of what we shall receive.
vv: I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory about to be revealed to us.
The man who writes this has known beatings and shipwreck (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). He is not speaking lightly of pain. He is weighing it against something.
for the creation was subjected to futility, not of its own will but by the will of the one who subjected it, in hope
Most commentators take “the one who subjected it” to be God, after the sin of Adam, when the ground was cursed (Genesis 3:17). The last two words matter most: even this subjection was “in hope”.
We know that the whole creation has been groaning in labor pains until now;
Labour pains hurt, but they are the pains of a birth. Paul does not say that the world is dying. He says that something is about to be born.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage to show the common destiny of the material world and of humanity (CCC 1046–1047). St Irenaeus uses it to teach that creation itself will be renewed and not thrown away (in substance; Against Heresies V, 32). Pope Francis recalls v. 22 at the opening of Laudato Si' (no. 2), saying that the earth itself is among the most abandoned and maltreated of our poor.

set: We are near the end of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). Jesus has already taught his disciples the Our Father (6:9–13) and has told them not to worry, because the Father knows their needs (6:25–33). Now he returns to prayer. Luke keeps a parallel in his own teaching on prayer (Luke 11:9–13), and there the Father's good gift is the Holy Spirit.
str: vv. 7–8: three commands and three promises.
vv. 9–11: two small examples from family life, and an argument from the lesser to the greater.
v. 12: the rule for how we treat others.
kw: All three Greek commands are in the present tense, which suggests continuing action: keep asking, keep searching, keep knocking.
A familiar way of arguing in Jewish teaching, from the small case to the great. If flawed parents know how to give, what of God?
The same phrase stands at 5:17, at the start of the Sermon's teaching on the Law. Together they frame everything between.
vv: “Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.
“It will be given” and “will be opened” do not name who acts, a way of speech that points reverently to God.
If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
Jesus says “who are evil” almost in passing, and he goes on to speak of our love for our children. Even wounded human love is a small window on the Father.
“In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.
The Book of Tobit has it in a negative form (4:15), and Rabbi Hillel is remembered for a similar saying. Jesus gives it as a positive command: do not wait, begin.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus teaches a filial boldness in prayer (CCC 2610), and it deals honestly with the complaint that our prayer is not heard (CCC 2735–2737). It also names this verse the Golden Rule, one of the rules that always apply in moral decisions (CCC 1789). St Augustine, writing to the widow Proba, says that God does not need to be told our wishes, but that in prayer our desire is stretched so we can receive what he wants to give (in substance).

qa: I have asked and knocked for years. Why has the door not opened?

The verse does not promise that we will get exactly what we name. It promises that the Father gives good things and never a stone. Paul can say a few lines later that “we do not know how to pray as we ought” (Romans 8:26). Keep praying, and if it helps, speak with a priest about what you are asking (CCC 2735–2737).
study: Where in my life am I groaning, and can I see it as labour rather than as an ending?
Which part of Matthew 7:7 do I find hardest to keep on doing: asking, searching or knocking?

lead: Today's readings ask who sets us at liberty. Paul says every person serves some master, and that the service of sin pays its wages in death, while God gives eternal life as a gift. In Matthew, a paralysed man is carried to Jesus, and before his legs are healed his sins are forgiven. The key words are slave, gift and authority.

set: Paul has been saying that where sin increased, grace abounded even more (5:20). Someone may then ask whether it matters how we behave. Romans 6 answers: in Baptism we died with Christ to sin (6:3–4). In this section Paul uses the picture of slavery, which every reader in a Roman city would know at first hand. He apologises for the comparison in v. 19. He is using a social fact to make a point, and is not approving of slavery.
str: v. 15: the question.
vv. 16–19: two masters; once slaves of sin, now of righteousness.
vv. 20–22: what each service produced: shame and death, or holiness and life.
v. 23: the summary: wages and gift.
kw: The word means one who belongs wholly to another. In Paul it can be a title of honour; he calls himself “a servant” of Jesus Christ in this very letter (Romans 1:1, where the Greek word is the same).
This was a word for a soldier's pay. Sin keeps its promises in the worst way: it pays exactly what it owes.
This is the opposite of wages. Nobody earns it. Paul sets the two words side by side on purpose.
vv: But thanks be to God that you, having once been slaves of sin, have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were entrusted,

Notice the unusual turn of phrase. Paul does not say the teaching was entrusted to them but that they were entrusted to the teaching. Many scholars think he has in mind the instruction given before Baptism.
So what advantage did you then get from the things of which you now are ashamed?
This is a question for a good examination of conscience. Paul does not argue from fear here. He asks what sin ever really gave us.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
The Malayalam POC divides the verses a little differently and puts the first half of this sentence at the end of v. 22.
ch: The Catechism says that the more we do what is good the freer we become, and that the choice of evil is an abuse of freedom that leads to “the slavery of sin” (CCC 1733). Death is a consequence of sin (CCC 1008). St Augustine often repeats that when God crowns our merits he is crowning his own gifts (in substance), and this is the sense of Paul's last verse (compare CCC 2006–2009).

r.h: Authority on earth to forgive sins
set: “His own town” is Capernaum, where Jesus has settled (4:13). Mark and Luke tell this story too, with the crowd and the opening of the roof (Mark 2:1–12; Luke 5:17–26). Matthew tells it briefly and keeps only what matters most: the faith of those who bring him, the word of forgiveness, the objection, and the sign.
str: vv. 1–2: the man is brought, and Jesus forgives him.
vv. 3–4: the scribes' thought and Jesus' question.
vv. 5–7: the sign: “Stand up”.
v. 8: the crowd glorifies God.
kw: The same word that Jesus speaks to the disciples on the sea (14:27). He speaks courage first, before the cure.
The crowds have already noticed this in his teaching (7:29). Now it reaches to sin itself.
Jesus' own title for himself. It recalls the figure in Daniel 7:13–14, to whom authority is given.
vv: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”
“Their faith” means the faith of those who carried him. Others can bring someone to Christ when that person cannot go alone, and this is what intercession does.
Then some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.”
They are thinking seriously, for only God forgives sins. Their objection states the very truth that the story reveals about Jesus (CCC 589).
When the crowds saw it, they were filled with awe, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.
Only Matthew ends this way, and the plural is striking. Many commentators hear in it the Church of Matthew's own day, in which this authority continues (compare 16:19; 18:18).
ch: The Catechism teaches that only God forgives sins, that Jesus exercises this divine power as Son of God, and that he gives it to men to exercise in his name (CCC 1441). It names Christ the physician of souls and bodies who forgave and healed this man, and it says that he wills his Church to continue this healing in the sacraments (CCC 1421). St Ambrose marvels at a Lord who pardons one person for the sake of others' merit (in substance; On Luke 5).

qa: Does Jesus mean that the man's illness was caused by his sins?
Not in this passage. Elsewhere Jesus rejects that simple link (John 9:2–3; Luke 13:1–5). Here he addresses the deepest need first, and then shows his authority by the healing that can be seen.
study: Who has carried me to Christ, and whom am I carrying now in my prayer?
Romans 6:21 asks what advantage sin ever gave me. How would I honestly answer before my next confession?

lead: Truth is the thread of today's readings. Paul says that no human failure can make God untrue to his word. Jesus asks his disciples to be so truthful that they need no oath. God's faithfulness comes first, and ours is meant to resemble it. The key words are faithfulness and Yes.

set: Paul has just told his fellow Jews that outward signs without obedience are not enough (2:17–29). The natural question follows: does this leave Israel with nothing? Paul is a Jew himself, and he will not allow that. He writes in the style called diatribe, a teacher's lively argument with an imagined objector, so the questions in this passage are not all his own opinions. Some of them he answers at once, and the longer answer comes in Romans 9–11.
str: vv. 1–2: is there any advantage in being a Jew? Much.
vv. 3–4: human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God's faithfulness.
vv. 5–6: is God then unjust to judge us? By no means.
vv. 7–8: may we do evil for the sake of good? Paul rejects it.
kw: The words God has spoken: the Scriptures and promises entrusted to Israel. The Church has received them from Israel's hands.
One Greek word covers both faith and faithfulness. Paul plays on it: God's pistis is not undone by human apistia.
A strong refusal, literally “may it not be”, which is a favourite of Paul in Romans. It occurs twice in this passage (vv. 4 and 6).
vv: For in the first place the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
Paul says this with pride and gratitude. Later in the letter he adds that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). The Church teaches the same (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).
What if some were unfaithful? Will their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?
Paul says “some”, not all. The question holds for every believer, and for Christians as much as for anyone.
“So that you may be justified in your words, and prevail in your judging.”
Paul quotes Psalm 51:4 in the Greek form, from David's great prayer of repentance. To admit our sin is to say that God is right.
And why not say (as some people slander us by saying that we say), “Let us do evil so that good may come”?
Some people were twisting Paul's preaching of grace into this slogan. He will have none of it.
ch: The Church has made v. 8 a rule of moral life: one may never do evil so that good may result from it (CCC 1756, 1789). It is a sentence for hard decisions, when a wrong act seems to offer a good result. Because God's faithfulness does not wait on ours, the sinner can always come back.

r.h: Let your word be Yes or No
set: This is the fourth of the six “you have heard, but I say” sayings of the Sermon on the Mount (5:21–48). The saying sums up what the Law taught: do not swear falsely, and keep your vows (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21). Jewish tradition itself was uneasy about careless swearing: Sirach warns against getting the habit (Sirach 23:9–11). Jesus takes this concern to its end.
str: v. 33: what was said.
vv. 34–36: do not swear at all; four examples.
v. 37: the rule: yes, no, and nothing more.
kw: To break an oath or to swear to something untrue. The Law forbade it, because God's name stood as guarantee.
People sometimes swore by heaven or Jerusalem rather than by God's name, as if this were a lesser thing (compare 23:16–22). Jesus shows that each of these belongs to God.
The Greek could also mean “from evil”, as in the last line of the Our Father (6:13).
vv: But I say to you, Do not swear at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God,
The images come from Isaiah 66:1 (heaven as throne, earth as footstool). You cannot step outside God's presence in order to make a promise on the side.
And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
This is a small and humorous touch. We cannot even control our own hair, so how could we offer it as a pledge?
Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one.
The need for an oath shows how little we trust one another. Jesus wants a community in which a plain word is enough. James repeats the teaching (James 5:12).
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage and explains that the Church's tradition, following St Paul (2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20), has not understood these words as excluding oaths taken for grave and right reasons, such as in court (CCC 2153–2154). St Augustine, commenting on the Sermon on the Mount, says that an oath is not a good thing to seek but may sometimes be needed because of the weakness of those who will not otherwise believe (in substance).

qa: May a Christian take an oath in court?

Yes, for a grave and right reason, as the Catechism says (CCC 2154). St Paul himself calls God to witness. What Jesus forbids is the careless use of God's name, and the double standard in which only a sworn word counts as true.
study: When did I last add “I swear” or something similar because my plain word was not enough? Why was that?
Where has God's faithfulness carried me through my own unfaithfulness?

lead: This Friday of the Great Fast has four readings. Genesis shows sin as something that grieves the heart of God. Joshua shows a new generation at Gilgal, where the disgrace of Egypt is rolled away, the Passover is kept and the manna stops. Paul says that the Law is holy, though it could not cure the illness it exposed. In the Temple, the authorities ask Jesus who gave him his authority, and they will not give an honest answer to his question. The key words are heart, new beginning and honesty.

r.h: It grieved him to his heart
set: The chapters between Eden and the flood show sin spreading: Cain's murder of Abel (4:8), Lamech's boast of vengeance (4:23–24), and now violence that fills the earth. Many scholars think the flood story weaves together two older accounts. This would explain why vv. 5–8 say “the Lord” and vv. 9–12 say “God”, with each telling the same situation in its own way.
str: vv. 5–7: what the Lord saw, felt and decided.
v. 8: the turning point: Noah.
vv. 9–10: who Noah was.
vv. 11–12: the earth as God saw it: corrupt and full of violence.
kw: From a verb for shaping, as a potter shapes clay. Later Jewish teachers built on this word to speak of the inner tendency to evil.
In v. 6 this is a word of deep feeling. Scripture speaks of God in human terms here, and also says that he does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19).
Grace. In Hebrew the consonants of this word are those of Noah's name reversed (nḥ and ḥn), a small wordplay in v. 8.
The sin the text names outright (v. 11). It is the opposite of the peace God intended among his creatures.
vv: And the Lord was sorry that he had made humankind on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.
Human “hearts” are named in v. 5 and the heart of God in v. 6. Sin is more than breaking a rule. It wounds a love.
But Noah found favor in the sight of the Lord.
This one short sentence holds back the destruction. It comes before we are told anything about what Noah did.
Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation; Noah walked with God.
Only Enoch has been said to walk with God (5:22–24). A person can be faithful even in a corrupt time.
ch: The Catechism uses these chapters when it says that after the first sin the world is virtually inundated by sin (CCC 401). On a Friday of the fast, the words about God's grieved heart lead us to the Cross, where the Church sees how far that grief and that love went.

r.h: The disgrace of Egypt is rolled away
set: Israel has crossed the Jordan on dry ground (Joshua 3–4), and the kings of the land are afraid. One would expect an army to attack at once. Instead the people stop at Gilgal, near Jericho, for two acts of worship. The generation that left Egypt has died in the wilderness, and those born on the way have not received the sign of the covenant.
str: v. 1: the kings' fear.
vv. 2–9: the circumcision at Gilgal.
vv. 10–12: the Passover, the produce of the land, and the end of the manna.
kw: Hebrew hears this verb in the name Gilgal, and v. 9 gives the wordplay. A place name becomes a memory of grace.
Slavery, and perhaps also the taunt that God could not bring them in. The text does not say exactly, but the burden is gone.
God's gift for the journey, as Exodus 16:35 said it would be, lasting until they reached the land.
vv: So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised;
The fathers' failure does not cancel God's plan. The promise passes to a new generation.
“Today I have rolled away from you the disgrace of Egypt.”
This is said before any battle. God gives them a new standing first, and they fight only afterwards.
The manna ceased on the day they ate the produce of the land,
The food for the journey ends when the journey ends. God does not keep his people as children for ever, and they now eat from the land he has given.
ch: Passover required circumcision (Exodus 12:48), so these two acts belong together. The Old Testament already speaks of a circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4), and the Letter to the Colossians speaks of it in Christ (Colossians 2:11). St Justin Martyr sees Joshua's second circumcision as a figure of what Christ does (in substance; Dialogue with Trypho 113). The Catechism sees Baptism prefigured in the crossing of the Jordan (CCC 1222) and the Eucharist in the manna (CCC 1094).

set: Paul has just said that Christians have “died to the law” (7:4). This could make it sound as if the Law were an evil thing, so he stops to defend it. For the first time in the letter he speaks at length in the first person. Most scholars do not read this as a diary of his own past, since he elsewhere calls himself blameless under the Law (Philippians 3:6). Many hear in this “I” the voice of Adam, or of Israel at Sinai, or of anyone who meets God's command and finds sin stirring.
str: v. 7: the question: is the Law sin? By no means.
vv. 8–11: how sin uses the commandment.
v. 12: the verdict: the Law is holy.
kw: The word for the wrong desire named in the last commandment (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21).
A military term for a base of operations. Sin occupies the good command as a base from which to attack.
The verb recalls the serpent's deception in the garden (Genesis 3:13), and this is one reason many hear Adam in this passage.
vv: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”
A sign that says “wet paint” does not make the paint wet, but it does show what is there, and often tempts us to touch.
and I died, and the very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
The fault is not in the command. Paul pins it on sin, which he speaks of almost as a person.
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.
Paul's verdict on the Law of his people is high praise. He never gives it up.
ch: The Catechism follows this passage closely: the Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet imperfect, for it shows what must be done but does not of itself give the strength of the Spirit to do it (CCC 1963). Only grace heals what the Law reveals.

set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem, and the day before, he drove the sellers from the Temple (11:15–18). Now, walking in the same courts, he is met by chief priests, scribes and elders, the groups he had said would reject him (8:31). “These things” most likely refers to what he did in the Temple. They were responsible for the Temple, and so their question was a natural one. It is about these leaders and this moment, and not about the Jewish people (CCC 597).
str: vv. 27–28: the question.
vv. 29–30: Jesus' counter-question about John.
vv. 31–32: their private discussion.
v. 33: no answer, and no answer in return.
kw: The word also appears in the people's first astonishment at Jesus (1:22). Mark's reader knows the answer.
A reverent way of saying “from God”.
These words are the point of the story. They do know what they think, but they choose not to say it.
vv: “By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?”
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? Answer me.
This is no trick. Their answer to John would have told them the answer about Jesus, since it was John who pointed to him.
They argued with one another, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’
They ask what will be safe to say, not what is true. This is what makes it impossible for them to learn.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.”
Jesus does not refuse honest doubt. He refuses to discuss with those who already will not say what they think.
ch: The Church honours John as the Lord's immediate forerunner, sent to prepare his way (CCC 523). The passage is also a lesson on conscience, the inner law that we are called to listen to (CCC 1776), and on truthfulness in speech and action (CCC 2468). In a good confession we do the opposite of “We do not know”: we say what we know.

qa: Did God really regret making human beings?

Genesis speaks of God in human language so that we may feel how seriously he takes sin. The Bible also says that he does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). The point is not that God made a mistake, but that sin matters to him, and that he remains faithful: he has already found Noah.
rite: The calendar's note for today asks for abstinence from meat and recommends fasting and the Way of the Cross. The first reading tells us why: the heart grieved in Genesis is the heart pierced on Calvary. Keep the fast according to your own eparchy's norms, and let the honest word of a good confession be part of it.
study: Do I think of sin as breaking a rule or as grieving a Father? What difference would it make?
What “disgrace of Egypt” do I want the Lord to roll away from me in this fast?
When have I said “I do not know” because the true answer would cost me something?

lead: At first these two readings seem to pull in opposite directions. Paul tells the Corinthians not even to eat with a member of the Church who persists in grave public sin. In Matthew, Jesus is mocked as “a friend of tax collectors and sinners”. Together they show that the Church must be both holy and merciful, and that discipline and table fellowship both exist so that sinners may come home. The key words are inside, outside and wisdom.

set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8), probably in the mid-50s, to a lively and divided church. A case has been reported of a Christian man living with his father's wife (5:1), and the community has done nothing about it, and is even proud of itself (5:2). Paul has told them to put him out so that “his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (5:5). These verses clear up a misunderstanding about something Paul had written earlier.
str: vv. 9–10: what the earlier letter did not mean.
v. 11: what it did mean.
vv. 12–13: the Church does not judge outsiders; a command from Deuteronomy.
kw: Literally “to mix up with”. It occurs only here and at 2 Thessalonians 3:14, and both places have to do with discipline among believers.
one who bears the name of brother or sister
The issue is someone who claims the name of Christian while openly contradicting it.
Those who are not members of the community. Paul does not retreat from them and does not condemn them.
vv: I wrote to you in my letter
This is an earlier letter that we no longer have. We are reading one side of a longer correspondence.
since you would then need to go out of the world.
Paul's Christians are not to form an escapist group. They are to live and work among all kinds of people, and to bear witness there.
Do not even eat with such a one.
Many scholars think this includes the shared meal at which the Lord's Supper was celebrated (11:17–34). The point is public witness and the sinner's conversion, not personal hatred.
For what have I to do with judging those outside?
The Church's discipline is for her own members. As for all others, “God will judge” (v. 13), and that spares us a critical spirit toward our neighbours.
ch: The last line of the passage repeats a formula from Deuteronomy (17:7 and elsewhere). The Church's discipline continues this concern. The Catechism explains that certain very grave sins incur excommunication, which bars one from the sacraments until absolution (CCC 1463). The purpose stated in 5:5 governs the whole: salvation, not punishment for its own sake.

set: John the Baptist is in prison (11:2). Jesus has just praised him as more than a prophet (11:7–15). Now he speaks about those of his time who would not respond to either of them. He draws his picture from what any child had seen: children in the market square playing at weddings and at funerals.
str: vv. 16–17: the picture: children whose friends will play neither game.
v. 18: John: fasting, and called a demoniac.
v. 19: the Son of Man: eating, and called a glutton. The closing saying on wisdom.
kw: A phrase for those of that time who refused the message. It is not a judgment on a whole people: John, Jesus and the first disciples were Jews, and many followed them.
An insult that has become one of the most beautiful titles of Jesus. Tax collectors were despised for working for the ruling powers.
In the Jewish wisdom books, Wisdom is God's own wise plan in person. Matthew goes on at once to have Jesus speak in Wisdom's voice (11:28–30; compare Sirach 51:23–27).
vv: We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not mourn.
The critics are like sulky children: whatever the tune, they will not play. Those who do not want to respond will always find a reason.
‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’
“A glutton and a drunkard” echoes Deuteronomy 21:20, a charge against a rebellious son. The insult reveals what Jesus was really doing: eating with those whom others avoided.
Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.

A note on the text. Luke has “by all her children” (7:35), and some manuscripts of Matthew read “children” here also, but “deeds” is the better reading in Matthew. God's plan will be shown right by what it produces.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus scandalized some of his hearers by eating with tax collectors and sinners (CCC 588) and that he invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom (CCC 545). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, points out that John and Jesus came by opposite roads, the strict one and the gentle one, so that nobody would have an excuse (in substance). John's fast and Jesus' table are not rivals. The Church has both a season of fasting and a feast at the end of it (compare Matthew 9:14–15).
