qa: Should I stop eating with a relative who is living in sin?

Paul is speaking about public discipline by the community in one grave and unrepentant case. He is not telling families to shun their members. Jesus ate with sinners, and Paul himself names the person's salvation as the aim (5:5). Keep the door open, keep the love real, do not pretend wrong is right, and ask your parish priest when a hard case arises.
study: Where do I judge those I have no business judging, and where do I stay silent when love should speak?
Am I more like the children who refuse every tune? What call of God have I been finding reasons to ignore?

lead: This Third Sunday of the Great Fast joins four readings that all ask the same thing: who saves us? Noah is saved inside the ark, and it is the Lord who shuts him in. Joshua asks an armed stranger whose side he is on, and learns that the real question is whether he is on God's side. Paul cries, “Who will rescue me?” and answers in the next line. On the road to Jerusalem Jesus speaks of his death, two disciples ask for thrones, and he answers with a cup and a ransom. The key words are inside, holy ground, rescue and serve. The forty days of rain belong to the Bible's long line of forties.

r.h: And the Lord shut him in
set: Genesis 1–11 speaks of beginnings: of the world, of sin and of God's patience. People in the ancient Near East told other flood stories, such as those in the Gilgamesh and Atrahasis epics. In Genesis the one God acts, with grief over sin and with care for one family and for every kind of creature. Many scholars think two older accounts have been woven together here, and this would explain small differences. For example, Noah takes seven pairs of clean animals in 7:2, while here they go in “two and two”. The rain lasts forty days in v. 12, while the waters swell for a hundred and fifty days in v. 24.
str: vv. 6–10: Noah's age, the entry into the ark, and the seven days.
vv. 11–12: the date and the bursting of the waters.
vv. 13–16: the entry told again, ending with the Lord closing the door.
vv. 17–20: the waters rise and the ark floats.
vv. 21–24: all flesh dies; only those in the ark remain.
kw: A special word used in the Old Testament almost only for this flood (the one other place is Psalm 29:10).

This word, which means a chest or box and not a ship, is used elsewhere only for the basket of the infant Moses (Exodus 2:3). In both, a small floating box holds God's future. The text mentions no rudder and no sail.
The deep of Genesis 1:2. God had separated the waters on the second day (1:6–7). Now the fountains below and the windows above open, as though creation were being undone.
vv: all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened.
The exact date in this verse gives a solemn, record-like tone. What sin began inwardly now breaks out in the whole of creation.
The rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights.
Forty is the Bible's number of testing and of new beginnings: Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:28), Elijah on the road (1 Kings 19:8) and Jesus in the desert (Matthew 4:2).
and the Lord shut him in.
This is the most tender line in the story. Noah does not close the door himself, and Genesis uses here the personal name of God, “the Lord”. Being saved is first of all God's act.
Only Noah was left, and those that were with him in the ark.
Here begins the Bible's idea of a remnant: through a few, God saves many. One family carries forward the future of the human race.
ch: The Catechism says that the Church is prefigured by Noah's ark, “which alone saves from the flood” (CCC 845), and it sees in the ark a prefiguring of Baptism, for eight persons “were saved through water” (CCC 1219; 1 Peter 3:20). St Augustine, in the City of God, reads the ark as a figure of the Church, and its door in the side as the wound in Christ's side (in substance; XV, 26). This image does not shut out those who do not know Christ through no fault of their own, as the Church also teaches (CCC 847).

r.h: The place where you stand is holy
set: Israel has crossed the Jordan and kept the Passover at Gilgal (5:10). Jericho stands closed before them. The book of Joshua took its final form long after the events it tells, and many scholars think it was shaped under the later kings or in the exile. Its purpose is to teach that the land is God's gift. Its stories of war belong to that ancient setting, and the Church reads them in the light of Christ, who “came not to be served”.
str: vv. 13–15: Joshua meets the commander of the army of the Lord.
6:1: Jericho is shut.
6:2–5: the Lord's strange orders: six days of marching, then seven priests, seven trumpets, seven circuits and a shout.
kw: commander of the army of the Lord
The “army” (the word in “Lord of hosts”) is heaven's army, and it is not Israel's. This figure comes from God and speaks with his authority.
This one small Hebrew word is the answer. Joshua's question has two choices, and neither is right.
The horn used in worship and at feasts (Leviticus 25:9) as well as in war. Here priests carry the horns before the ark, so the march looks more like a liturgical procession than a siege.
vv: “Are you one of us, or one of our adversaries?”
It is the natural question, and it is ours too. We tend to ask God to take our side in every quarrel.
“Neither; but as commander of the army of the Lord I have now come.”
The real question is the other way around: are we on God's side?
“Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy.”
These are nearly the words spoken to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5). The new leader begins as the old leader began, barefoot.
and the wall of the city will fall down flat,
Nothing here depends on siege engines. The first victory in the land is a gift, received in obedience. Hebrews 11:30 says that it was “by faith”.
ch: Early Christian writers such as St Justin Martyr and Origen saw in this commander the Word of God himself, coming to meet the man who shares his name (in substance). Hebrews 4:8 shows the link, because in Greek the names Joshua and Jesus are the same. Origen also reads Jericho as this world of sin, whose walls fall through the trumpet of the Gospel (in substance; Homilies on Joshua). The caption given to this reading takes the same line: the walls of wickedness fall by the Lord's power.

set: After defending the Law (7:7–13), Paul describes what it is like to know the good and still fail to do it. He continues in the first person, and now in the present tense. The Roman poet Ovid has a similar line about seeing the better and following the worse (Metamorphoses 7), so the experience is not only a Christian one.
str: v. 14: spiritual Law, sold self.
vv. 15–20: the same experience stated twice: I do what I do not want.
vv. 21–23: two laws at war.
vv. 24–25: the cry, the thanks, and a last summary.
kw: This does not mean the body as bad. In Paul it means human nature left to itself and turned away from God. So “in my flesh” (v. 18) does not condemn our bodies, which are to be raised.
The part of a person that truly delights in God's law (v. 22). Sin has not destroyed it.
This is a cry of misery, and not of despair, for the answer is already coming.
To pull someone out of danger. The verb is in the Our Father: “rescue us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13).
vv: I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
Every honest person knows this verse. This is the state in which many of us come to the Great Fast, and it is where grace begins.
For I delight in the law of God in my inmost self,
Paul does not say that human beings are totally corrupt. The longing for good is real. The trouble is the power to carry it out.
Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?
He asks “who” and not “what”. No method can answer this question, only a person.
Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!
This is the answer, and Romans 8:1–2 develops it: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”.
ch: The Catechism draws on this passage when it speaks of the gap between wanting and doing (CCC 2542). It teaches that concupiscence, the inclination to sin, remains in the baptized as a struggle to be fought with the help of grace (CCC 1264, 2515), and that human nature is wounded but not totally corrupted (CCC 405). St Augustine at first took this “I” as a person under the Law, and later as the believer who still struggles (in substance). Both readings are found in the tradition.

r.h: To give his life a ransom for many
set: Jesus has left Galilee and is going up to Jerusalem. This is the third time in Matthew that he foretells his Passion (16:21; 17:22–23), and it is the most detailed; here for the first time he says “crucified”. Immediately after this comes the mother's request. Mark tells that James and John ask for themselves (Mark 10:35); Matthew has their mother ask with them. She will appear once more, looking on from a distance at the Cross (27:55–56).
str: vv. 17–19: the third foretelling.
vv. 20–21: the request.
vv. 22–23: the cup.
v. 24: the anger of the ten.
vv. 25–28: true greatness; the ransom.
kw: In the Prophets and Psalms, the cup can be the cup of God's judgment (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17). Jesus will pray about it in Gethsemane (26:39).
Two words for rising in the kingdom by going down. “Deacon” comes from the first.
The price paid to release a captive or a slave. Compare the Servant who “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12).
“Many” in this Semitic way of speaking does not mean “some but not all”. The Catechism says that this term is not restrictive, but contrasts the whole of humanity with the one Redeemer (CCC 605).
vv: and on the third day he will be raised.”
Every foretelling ends here. Jesus goes to Jerusalem knowing both the worst and the end.
one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.”
Matthew will use the same picture at Calvary, where two bandits are crucified, “one on his right and one on his left” (27:38). This is what the place beside this King looks like.
“You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.”
They mean it, and they do not yet know what they are saying. They will run away (26:56), and Jesus will still keep his word.
He said to them, “You will indeed drink my cup,
James was the first of the Twelve to die for Christ (Acts 12:2). Tradition says that John lived long and bore witness to old age. There is more than one way to drink this cup.
just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
Daniel's Son of Man was to be served by all peoples (Daniel 7:14). Jesus keeps the title and turns it around. This is the reason for the rule in vv. 26–27: the Master has done it first.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse to explain that the Redemption consists in Christ's giving his life as a ransom (CCC 622), and that this was for all (CCC 605). It teaches that ministry in the Church is service (CCC 876, 1551). The Second Vatican Council says of the Church's mission that Christ entered this world to serve and not to be served (Gaudium et Spes 3).

qa: Did the flood really cover the whole earth?

The Church asks us to attend to the literary form and purpose of each biblical text (Dei Verbum 12; CCC 110). Genesis 1–11 tells of real truths: God's holiness, the seriousness of sin, his mercy, and his covenant. It uses images and forms of its own time to do so, and it does not set out to give modern geography or science. Catholics do not have to prove a world-wide flood in order to believe what the passage teaches.
To whom was the ransom paid? To the devil?

St Gregory of Nazianzus takes up this question and rejects both answers: it was not paid to the evil one, and God the Father did not demand it as a price (in substance; Oration 45). “Ransom” is an image for what it cost to set us at liberty, and for the love that paid it (CCC 601, 622).
Is Paul in Romans 7 saying that I cannot help sinning?

No. He is describing the struggle honestly, and the very next chapter speaks of the Spirit's power. Grace does not remove every struggle at once, but it enables us to win (CCC 1264, 1987–1989). A person who falls should neither despair nor stop trying. The Lord waits in the sacrament of Reconciliation.
rite: In the Syro-Malabar Church, the second reading has a particular force for us. Joshua's Hebrew name, Yehoshua, is the same name as that of Jesus, whom we call Isho in the form that comes to us through Syriac. Many of our people still leave their footwear at the church door, and so say what Joshua learned. When we receive from the kasa in the Holy Qurbana, we answer the Lord's question with James and John: by your grace, we are able. We then go out from the Qurbana to serve, because we have been served at the table of the One who gave his life.
study: What in my life still needs the Lord to “shut the door” for me? Where am I trying to save myself?
Before my next quarrel, can I ask Joshua's question the other way around: am I on God's side?
In Romans 7:24 Paul asks “who”, not “what”. Which of my resolutions have I been treating as my saviour?
Jesus says the great are servants. Whom in my own home or parish have I been expecting to serve me?

lead: Both readings ask what a commandment is for. Paul says that the baptized have died to the law as a way of being saved, and now serve God in the new life of the Spirit. In Mark a scribe asks Jesus which commandment comes first, and the two of them end in agreement: love of God and love of neighbour stand above everything else. Neither reading throws the law away. Both go to its heart. For the Great Fast the question is plain: do my fasting and prayer come from love, or only from duty?

set: Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, probably from Corinth, around AD 57. In chapter 6 he has said that the baptized died to sin with Christ. Now he applies the same thought to the law of Moses, speaking “to those who know the law” (7:1). He is not attacking the law. A few verses later he says, “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (7:12). His point is that the law, good as it is, cannot itself give the power to keep it.
str: v. 1: the principle: law binds a person only during life.
vv. 2–3: an example from marriage: a death ends the bond.
v. 4: the application: you died to the law through Christ’s body, to belong to another.
vv. 5–6: then and now: fruit for death, and service in the Spirit.
¶ The example does not match at every point: in the marriage the husband dies, in the application we do. Paul wants only one thing from it: a death ends one obligation and makes a new bond possible.
kw: The verb of 7:2 and 7:6. It means to make something no longer effective. The law is not destroyed; the person is released from its claim.
Used in v. 4 and again in v. 5. Everyone bears fruit of some kind. The question is for whom: “for God” or “for death”.
The NRSV has “the new life of the Spirit”. The Greek contrasts the newness of Spirit with the oldness of the letter, and the Malayalam POC keeps that contrast of new and old.
vv: In the same way, my friends, you have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead
The body of Christ here is first his crucified body, into whose death we were baptized (6:3–4). The image is still marriage: the Christian life is above all belonging to a person, the Risen One.
But now we are discharged from the law, dead to that which held us captive, so that we are slaves not under the old written code but in the new life of the Spirit.
Paul still says “slaves”. Service has not ended, but its source has changed: not fear of a written code, but the Spirit living within us.
ch: The Catechism says that the Old Law is holy, and that according to St Paul its special function is to denounce and disclose sin (CCC 1963). The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ (CCC 1965–1966). St Augustine wrote a whole treatise on this contrast, The Spirit and the Letter: the law commands, and grace gives the power to do what it commands (in substance). Paul speaks here about what can save us. He passes no judgement on the Jewish people or on their love of the Torah.

set: Jesus is in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. A series of disputes has been running since 11:27: about his authority, about taxes, about the resurrection. This scribe, an expert in the Law, comes to him differently: he has listened and sees “that he answered them well”. Matthew and Luke tell of a similar question as a test (Matthew 22:35; Luke 10:25). Only Mark has this warm exchange.

Jesus answers with Scripture his hearers knew by heart. Deuteronomy 6:4–5 is the opening of the Shema, which devout Jews prayed morning and evening and pray still. Leviticus 19:18 gives the love of neighbour.
str: v. 28: the question: which commandment is first?
vv. 29–31: the answer: he is asked for one and gives two.
vv. 32–33: the scribe repeats it and draws a conclusion about sacrifice.
v. 34: “You are not far”, and the end of all questions.
kw: The first word of the Shema. In Hebrew, to hear includes to obey. Love begins with listening to the God who speaks.
A love that is a matter of will and action, more than of feeling. Heart, soul, mind and strength together mean the whole person, nothing held back.
This word appears only here in the New Testament. It suggests having a mind that has grasped the point.
vv: The first is, ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one;

Jesus begins with who God is, before he says what we must do. Love of God flows from faith in the one God. Both commandments he gives come from Israel’s own Scripture: he is opening up the treasure of his people, not replacing it.
this is much more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.
The scribe says this inside the Temple. He stands in the line of the prophets: compare Hosea 6:6 and 1 Samuel 15:22. Worship is not rejected. Sacrifice without love is what is emptied of value.
You are not far from the kingdom of God.
Praise, and also an invitation. The scribe has understood the commandment. What remains is the step toward the one who is speaking to him. The reader of Mark is left to ask whether he took it.
ch: The Catechism takes this answer as the summary of our duties to God (CCC 2083) and of the whole Law (CCC 2196), and it reads the Shema as the foundation of faith in the one God (CCC 228). Pope Benedict XVI opens Deus Caritas Est by noting that Jesus united the command of love of God with that of love of neighbour (Deus Caritas Est 1).

qa: If we have died to the law, do Christians still need the commandments?

Yes. Paul himself says that “love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:10). What has ended is the idea that a written code can save us by itself. The Catechism recalls that the Ten Commandments still bind Christians (CCC 2068), and the Spirit gives the strength to keep them from the heart.
study: What do I do in this Great Fast only out of duty? How could love become its reason?
“You are not far.” What one step toward Christ am I still putting off?

lead: Two warnings, both from people who love their hearers. Paul tells Christians who feel secure in their baptism and their Eucharist that Israel, too, was blessed and yet fell in the desert. In Luke, Jesus teaches that the day of the Son of Man can come like a trap on a heart made heavy with pleasure or worry. Each warning ends in hope: God is faithful and gives a way out, and prayer gives the strength to stand. Watchfulness is the work of the Fast.

set: Paul writes to Corinth from Ephesus (16:8) in the mid-50s. Chapters 8–10 deal with food offered to idols and with meals in pagan temples. Some Corinthians feel safe: they have “knowledge” (8:1), they are baptized, and they share the Lord’s table. Paul answers from the story of the Exodus: our ancestors had their gifts too, and that did not keep them from falling.
str: vv. 1–4: all of them received God’s gifts: the word “all” comes five times.
v. 5: yet most of them fell in the wilderness.
vv. 6–10: warnings from that story: idolatry, immorality, testing the Lord, complaining.
vv. 11–12: why it was written: “to instruct us”.
v. 13: the comfort: God is faithful.
kw: The word in v. 6 (and the adverb in v. 11). A typos is the mark left by a blow or a seal. The Church’s word for this way of reading, “typology”, comes from it: the events of Israel are real history and also carry an imprint of what God does in Christ.
The Greek word covers both. The NRSV says “testing”; the Malayalam POC says temptation. The same event can be a test sent to strengthen us, and an enemy’s attempt to bring us down.
An exit, the way out of a narrow pass. God does not promise that there will be no trial. He promises a door within it.
vv: and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.

Israel drank water from the rock in Exodus 17 and Numbers 20. Later Jewish tradition told of a rock or well that travelled with the people, and Paul may be drawing on this. His claim is bolder: Christ was already there, giving life to his people in the desert.
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did, and were destroyed by serpents.

A note on the text: the ancient manuscripts differ here. Some read “Christ”, as the NRSV does; others read “the Lord”, as the Malayalam POC does. In v. 8, Paul’s “twenty-three thousand” differs from the twenty-four thousand of Numbers 25:9, perhaps quoted from memory. His lesson is the same in either case.
So if you think you are standing, watch out that you do not fall.
This is the centre of the passage. The danger is not only sin but the feeling of being beyond it.
God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it.
The last word belongs to God’s faithfulness. The way out is not always an escape: Paul says that it comes so that we may be able to endure.
ch: The Catechism uses this chapter to show how the Church reads the Old Testament in the light of Christ: the crossing of the sea is a type of baptism (CCC 117), and the water from the rock is a figure of Christ’s spiritual gifts (CCC 1094). Its teaching on “lead us not into temptation” asks for this same vigilance (CCC 2846–2849). St Augustine, preaching on the Psalms, says that our pilgrimage cannot be without temptation, for we make progress through it, and no one knows himself unless he is tried (Expositions on the Psalms 60; in substance).

r.h: That day need not be a trap
set: These are the last words of the discourse that Jesus gives in the Temple (21:5–36), on the destruction of Jerusalem and the coming of the Son of Man. Many scholars think that Luke wrote after the city fell in AD 70, and his account distinguishes that event from the end of all things. After the frightening signs he has said, “your redemption is drawing near” (21:28). Now he tells his hearers how to live in the meantime.
str: vv. 29–31: the parable of the fig tree and all the trees.
vv. 32–33: this generation; words that will not pass away.
vv. 34–35: “Be on guard”: a heart weighed down.
v. 36: “Be alert”: prayer, strength, standing before the Son of Man.
kw: The heavy head left by a drinking bout. The word occurs only here in the New Testament. Jesus names something ordinary, and joins it to “the worries of this life”.
The same word is used of the “cares” that choke the seed in the Gospel’s explanation of the sower (Luke 8:14). A respectable worry can make a heart as heavy as a bad habit.
Literally, stay awake. The present tense suggests a continuing state, not a moment of alarm.
vv: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
Isaiah said this of God’s word: “the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus says it of his own.
Be on guard so that your hearts are not weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the worries of this life,
The danger is a sleepy heart more than a dramatic sin. This is why the Fast touches food, drink and the crowded mind.
Be alert at all times, praying that you may have the strength to escape all these things that will take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.
To stand is the opposite of being crushed and of falling. Prayer is what gives the strength, and to stand before him is the goal.
ch: The Catechism counts this text among those where Jesus calls his hearers to watchfulness in prayer (CCC 2612). Since the Ascension, it says, Christ’s coming has been “imminent”, even though it is not for us to know the times (CCC 673). So each Holy Qurbana is offered in expectation: we proclaim the Lord’s death “until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

qa: Was Jesus mistaken when he said “this generation will not pass away”?

The verse has been explained in more than one way. Some scholars take “generation” to be those who saw the fall of Jerusalem, one great sign of the things Jesus foretold. Others take it to mean humanity, or the people of faith, who will last to the end. Jesus himself says that no one but the Father knows the day or the hour (Mark 13:32), so he gives no date. The Church’s teaching on watchfulness does not depend on any one of these explanations.
study: Where do I feel most “safe” in my faith? What does 1 Corinthians 10:12 say to that feeling?
Which worry is making my heart heavy this week? How can I bring it to prayer?

lead: Today’s readings ask for the hardest thing in Christian life. The First Letter of Peter tells Christians who are being insulted not to repay evil with evil, but with a blessing. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, “Love your enemies”, and gives the reason: this is what the Father does every morning when the sun comes up. Fasting that does not reach the way we treat those who wrong us has not reached far enough.

set: The letter is addressed to believers scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor (1:1). They are a small minority, and they suffer insults and suspicion because of their new way of life (2:12; 4:4). It names Peter as its author. Many scholars think a disciple gave it its final form in his name, while others hold that Peter wrote it with the help of Silvanus (5:12). After instructions for particular groups (2:18–3:7), the writer now turns to “all of you”.
str: v. 8: five qualities of a Christian community.
v. 9: the rule: no evil for evil, but a blessing.
vv. 10–12: support from Psalm 34:12–16, quoted in its Greek form.
kw: The NRSV has “unity of spirit”. It does not mean thinking the same about everything. It means sharing the one mind of those who belong to Christ.
In the Greek world of the time, being “lowly” was generally no compliment. The Christians made it a virtue, because of the Lord they followed.
Literally, to speak well of. The answer to abuse is a good word, spoken to God and to others about the one who did the wrong.
vv: Do not repay evil for evil or abuse for abuse; but, on the contrary, repay with a blessing.
The letter has already shown where this comes from: “When he was abused, he did not return abuse” (2:23). It is the way Jesus himself walked.
let them turn away from evil and do good; let them seek peace and pursue it.
Peace is something to run after. The psalm does not tell us to wait for it to arrive. It tells us to go and find it, and often the first step is ours.
For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer.
Why can someone leave vengeance aside? Because the matter is in God’s sight. Nothing done to them goes unseen, and the prayer of the wronged is heard.
ch: This teaching was known very early. St Polycarp, who died a martyr in old age, repeats the line about not returning evil for evil in his letter to the Philippians (chapter 2). The Catechism teaches that Christ’s disciples are to forgive from the heart, and that Christian prayer extends even to the forgiveness of enemies, which is a high point of that prayer (CCC 2843–2844).

r.h: So that you may be children of your Father
set: This is the last of six sayings in the Sermon on the Mount that begin “You have heard” (5:21–48). Jesus has said that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (5:17), and here he goes to its deepest intention.

“You shall love your neighbor” is Leviticus 19:18. “Hate your enemy” is not a commandment of the Law of Moses. The Law itself says that an enemy’s stray animal must be brought back (Exodus 23:4), and Proverbs says to feed a hungry enemy (Proverbs 25:21). Jesus may be answering a popular way of limiting the word “neighbour”. Many scholars also recall that one community of that age, at Qumran, taught its members to hate “the sons of darkness”.
str: v. 43: what they have heard.
v. 44: the command: love, and pray.
v. 45: the reason: the Father’s sun and rain.
vv. 46–47: two questions: what more are you doing?
v. 48: the summary: as your Father is.
kw: The verb does not ask us to feel fondness. It asks us to will the other’s good and to act for it. That is why it can be commanded.
“What more are you doing?” Christian life is measured by what goes beyond the ordinary exchange of favours.

It suggests what is complete and whole, with a whole heart, not faultless performance. Luke’s version of the saying reads, “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). In context, perfection means loving as God does, without limits.
vv: But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

Prayer is where this starts, when feeling will not cooperate. It is hard to go on hating someone we bring to God day after day. Jesus did this on the cross (Luke 23:34), and Stephen did it as he died (Acts 7:60).
for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the righteous and on the unrighteous.

In a land that depends on rain, this was the plainest evidence of all. God’s goodness does not wait to be earned. To love like this is to look like our Father, and children are known by their likeness.
Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
The Second Vatican Council takes this verse as the call of every Christian to holiness (Lumen Gentium 40). It is meant for families and workplaces, not only for monasteries.
ch: The Catechism says that charity reaches even to enemies (CCC 1825), and quotes this command of Jesus when it teaches on anger and hatred (CCC 2303). Every Christian is called to holiness on the basis of this verse (CCC 2013). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, describes the steps by which Jesus leads us upward: not to begin the wrong, not to avenge it, to bear it, to do good to the one who did it, and at last to pray for him (Homilies on Matthew 18; in substance).

qa: Does loving my enemy mean that I must accept injustice or stay in danger?

No. To love is to want the other’s true good, and it is no good for a wrongdoer to go on doing wrong. The Church teaches that a person may legitimately defend life (CCC 2264), and those who are being harmed may seek safety and justice. What Jesus forbids is hatred and revenge (CCC 2302–2303). Forgiveness can begin as a prayer long before the feelings follow.
study: Whom do I find hardest to pray for? Can I name that person before God today?
“What more are you doing?” Where has my love stayed only among those who love me?

lead: Both readings ask who is served by what we do. The Letter to the Ephesians enters an ancient household, with its children and fathers, slaves and masters, and tells each of them to act “as to the Lord”. In Mark, Jesus asks who the Messiah really is, and then warns against religious men who use their office for honour and profit, even at the cost of widows. On the day of Blessed Rani Maria, a sister who spent her life among the poor, the contrast is easy to see.

set: This passage is the end of a “household code” that began at 5:21 with the words “Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ”. Similar lists are found in Colossians 3:18–4:1 and 1 Peter 2:18–3:7, and ancient moral writers discussed the household in much the same way. What is new is the Lord in the midst of it, and the fact that duties run in both directions. Children and slaves are addressed directly, as members of the Church.

The letter is received in the Church as from Paul, writing from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think that a disciple wrote it in his name, while others defend Paul’s authorship. In either case the Church reads it as inspired Scripture.
str: vv. 1–3: children: obedience and the commandment with a promise.
v. 4: fathers: no provocation; formation in the Lord.
vv. 5–8: slaves: service from the heart, as to Christ.
v. 9: masters: the same to them; one Master over both.
kw: Roman law gave a father very great power over his household. Paul’s word to fathers places a limit on that power, and takes the child’s heart seriously.
Formation by training and by the spoken word. The phrase “of the Lord” says what kind of formation it is, and whose.
Literally, receiving the face: judging by a person’s outward position. The Malayalam POC’s മുഖംനോട്ടം catches this exactly. God does not look at rank.
vv: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
“In the Lord” sets both the ground of this obedience and its limit. The next verse quotes the commandment on honouring father and mother (Exodus 20:12).
And, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
A single verse for the father’s whole task: not to crush, and to form. Children often learn who God is from how their parents treat them.
Render service with enthusiasm, as to the Lord and not to men and women,
This phrase has given dignity to all sorts of hidden work. It does not bless the condition of slavery; it says that no human being finally owns another person’s service.
for you know that both of you have the same Master in heaven, and with him there is no partiality.
In the ancient world this was a startling thing to say to a slave owner, and it carried a force that later generations would at last draw out.
ch: The Catechism sets out the duties of children (CCC 2214–2220) and of parents (CCC 2221–2231): by obeying the Father themselves, parents teach their children to keep God’s law, and they are the first educators of their children (CCC 2222–2223). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, urges parents to raise their child as an athlete for Christ (Homilies on Ephesians 21; in substance).

set: The questions have ended (12:34), and now Jesus asks one himself, in the Temple. Many of his people expected a Messiah from David’s line, according to God’s promise (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus does not deny this. He asks whether “son of David” says enough. He uses Psalm 110, which was attributed to David, as the people of his time read it. Then he speaks to the crowd about their teachers. Right after this reading comes the poor widow who gives all she has (12:41–44).
str: vv. 35–37a: the Messiah: David’s son and David’s Lord.
v. 37b: the crowd listens with delight.
vv. 38–39: what certain scribes love: robes, greetings, seats.
v. 40: what they do: widows’ houses and long prayers.
kw: In the Greek of the psalm the same word stands for both: “The Lord said to my Lord”. The Hebrew uses God’s name first, then ’ādôn, a word for a master or a king. The early Christians heard in this the risen Jesus, seated at God’s right hand.
Dignified garments that made a teacher noticed. The problem is not the clothing but the love of being seen in it.

Many scholars think of teachers who took advantage of the trust of widows, for example in managing their property. The Law had a special care for widows (Deuteronomy 24:17), which is why this offence is so grave.
vv: David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son?
Jesus leaves the riddle open. A Christian knows the answer: son of David according to the flesh, and Son of God raised in power (Romans 1:3–4).
Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes,

Mark has just shown a scribe who is not far from the kingdom (12:34), so this is no blanket judgement on a whole group. The warning goes to every holder of religious office in any age, and it applies first of all to our own clergy, catechists and parish leaders.
They devour widows’ houses and for the sake of appearance say long prayers.
Prayer used as a screen is, for Jesus, among the worst of abuses. Even a fast can be kept for appearance (Matthew 6:16).
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus claims the title of Lord in a veiled way when he raises Psalm 110 here (CCC 447). The verse “Sit at my right hand” became one of the texts most often quoted in the New Testament, and the Creed echoes it in every Holy Qurbana. Pastors are reminded that authority in the Church is service (CCC 876).

qa: Does Ephesians approve of slavery?

The letter speaks inside a world where slavery was taken for granted, and tiny communities had no power to change the law. It does not attack the institution. It does plant what would one day undo it: one Master over both, no partiality, and in another letter a slave received as “a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). St Gregory of Nyssa was already condemning the owning of human beings in the fourth century (Homilies on Ecclesiastes 4; in substance). The Church now teaches plainly that enslaving human beings is gravely wrong (Gaudium et Spes 27; CCC 2414). This text must never be used to defend it.
rite: Today the Syro-Malabar Church remembers Blessed Rani Maria Vattalil, a Franciscan Clarist sister from Pulluvazhy, who worked among poor tribal families around Udainagar in the diocese of Indore. She helped them to learn, to save, and to stand up to the debts that held them down. On 25 February 1995 she was stabbed to death on a journey by bus, killed by a man hired by those who were losing from her work. Today’s Gospel warns against those who devour the houses of the poor; her life defended them. And what followed is a lesson for the Great Fast: her family forgave the man, who had repented in prison. Her sister visited him and received him as a brother, and her parents welcomed him to their home. She was beatified at Indore on 4 November 2017.
study: Whose service in my home or work do I accept without noticing? How can I thank that person, and how can my own work be done “as to the Lord”?
Where might I enjoy being seen as religious more than I enjoy serving? What would Blessed Rani Maria’s example ask of me?

lead: Four readings on this Friday of the Fast, and their common thread is life that God holds on to. After the flood God binds himself by a covenant with every living creature. At Jericho a wall falls before patient obedience, and one household is spared. Paul announces that there is “no condemnation” for those in Christ, for the Spirit gives life. And Jesus tells the Sadducees that God is the God of the living, so that even death does not break his bond with those he loves. The second reading contains one of the hardest pages in the Bible, and the Church does not hide it: see the question below.

set: The flood is over, and Noah has come out of the ark. God blesses him with the words of creation, “Be fruitful and multiply” (9:1), so this is a new beginning for the world. Many scholars think that this part of Genesis received its final form among priests around the time of the Babylonian exile, when Israel needed to hear that God’s promise outlasts disaster. It is the first covenant the Bible describes in full.
str: vv. 8–11: the covenant: with Noah, his descendants and all creatures.
vv. 12–16: the sign: the bow, which God himself will see and remember.
v. 17: the summary.
kw: A solemn bond. Here it is one-sided: God alone promises and asks nothing in return. The word “covenant” comes seven times in this reading.
The ordinary Hebrew word for a warrior’s bow. Many commentators see God hanging up his weapon in the sky after the storm.
In the Bible, for God to remember means to act faithfully. The sign is given so that God, in the language of the story, will see it and keep his word.
vv: I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood,
The promise is made after the flood has shown that the human heart is unchanged (8:21). God’s fidelity, not our goodness, is what holds the world in being.
When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.
The bond reaches the animals and the earth as well as human beings, a point that the Church has come to hear with new attention in our time.
ch: The Catechism says that this covenant stands for as long as the world lasts (CCC 71), and that it expresses God’s plan for the nations (CCC 56–58). Noah’s ark prefigures salvation by baptism (CCC 1094, 1219; 1 Peter 3:20–21).

r.h: The wall and the household of Rahab
set: Israel has crossed the Jordan (Joshua 3–4), and Jericho, one of the oldest cities in the world, stands before them. The story is told more like a liturgy than a battle: priests, trumpets, the ark, silence, seven days. Before this, the spies have been hidden by Rahab, a woman of the city (Joshua 2).

Many archaeologists find little sign of a large walled city at Jericho in the likely time of Joshua, and many scholars think that the book took shape centuries later, with a religious purpose. These matters remain under discussion.
str: vv. 8–11: the first day: one circuit in silence.
vv. 12–14: six days, one circuit each.
vv. 15–19: the seventh day: seven circuits; the command about the devoted things and Rahab.
vv. 20–21: the shout, the wall, the destruction.
vv. 22–25: Rahab and her family are spared.
vv. 26–27: Joshua’s oath and his fame.
kw: A thing or a city given over wholly to God, so that no one may profit from it. Other ancient peoples of the region had a similar practice in war, so this reflects the cruel customs of that age. See the question below.
The trumpet of Israel’s worship, not a military bugle. The word is used in 6:8 and is still sounded in the synagogue today.
The word reminds us that this is a page from a violent world, read by us in the light of the one who told Peter to put away his sword (Matthew 26:52).
vv: You shall not shout or let your voice be heard, nor shall you utter a word, until the day I tell you to shout.
Six days of walking and silence with nothing to show. The people must trust without seeing any result. This is a true picture of the Fast.
and the wall fell down flat;
The Letter to the Hebrews says, “By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days” (Hebrews 11:30). It is faith that the Church draws from this story.
But Rahab the prostitute, with her family and all who belonged to her, Joshua spared.

An outsider, and a woman of low repute, is the one who is saved along with her household. Hebrews praises her faith (11:31), James her works (James 2:25), and Matthew puts her in the family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
ch: The early Church read this page spiritually. St Clement of Rome saw in Rahab’s scarlet cord (Joshua 2:18) a sign of redemption through the Lord’s blood (1 Clement 12). Origen took the fall of Jericho as a picture of the world’s strongholds falling before the trumpet of the Gospel, and he saw in Rahab’s house an image of the Church (Homilies on Joshua 3 and 7; in substance).

set: Romans 7 ended with a cry: “Wretched man that I am!” (7:24). Chapter 8 is the answer. In the whole letter “Spirit” has come rarely so far; now it fills this chapter. Paul turns from the struggle of a person left to himself to the life of someone in Christ.
str: vv. 1–2: no condemnation: a new law, of the Spirit of life.
vv. 3–4: what God has done by sending his Son.
vv. 5–6: two ways of setting the mind.
kw: A legal word: the sentence and the penalty that follows it. It is the first thing Paul says about life in Christ.
In Paul this word is not the body as something bad. It is the whole person closed in on self, away from God. The Malayalam POC varies in rendering it, using words for both body and flesh.
What a person’s thoughts and desires lean toward. Fasting trains exactly this: it turns attention.
vv: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
The word “now” carries the whole Gospel. For the one who is in Christ the verdict has already been changed, and this is the ground of all our effort.
by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and to deal with sin, he condemned sin in the flesh,
“Likeness” is carefully chosen. The Son truly shares our condition, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). What was condemned on the cross was sin, not the sinner.
To set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace.
Paul does not set out a list of rules here. He asks where the heart is turned, and tells us what comes of it.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law is “the grace of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1965–1966), as St Thomas Aquinas taught when he said that the New Law consists chiefly in that grace (Summa Theologiae I–II, q. 106, a. 1; in substance). On “the likeness of sinful flesh”, see CCC 602.

set: This is the only appearance of the Sadducees in Mark. They were a priestly and aristocratic party in Jerusalem who, according to Acts 23:8 and the historian Josephus, denied the resurrection. They appealed to the Law of Moses, and they build their case on the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), by which a man married his childless brother’s widow to carry on the family line. Their story is meant to make belief in the resurrection look absurd.
str: v. 18: who they are.
vv. 19–23: the case of the seven brothers.
v. 24: Jesus’ reply: neither the scriptures nor the power of God.
v. 25: God’s power: risen life is not this life prolonged.
vv. 26–27: Scripture: the burning bush.
kw: Literally a standing up again. Many Jews of Jesus’ time, the Pharisees among them, hoped for it (see Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7).
The Sadducees imagine only what is possible for human beings. Jesus says they have left out what God can do.
The last word of the argument. God’s name is bound to persons who, from Moses’ point of view, were long dead, and he is still their God.
vv: Is not this the reason you are wrong, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?
The Catechism quotes this answer when it teaches on the resurrection (CCC 993). Both mistakes are still common: not to read the Word closely, and to make God as small as what we have seen.
For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
Jesus does not say that the love of a husband and wife is lost. He says that risen life is not arranged as this life is, with its need of heirs. Their riddle assumes too small a heaven.
He is God not of the dead, but of the living;

Jesus argues from Exodus 3:6, in the books the Sadducees themselves honour. God does not say “I was” the God of Abraham. A God who has bound himself to a person does not let that bond end at the grave.
ch: “Faith in the resurrection rests on faith in God” who is the God of the living (CCC 993). The Catechism also sees consecrated virginity, which it links to this verse, as a sign of the world to come (CCC 1619). This is the hope with which the Church prays for her dead at every Holy Qurbana.

qa: How can the Bible say that God ordered the destruction of a whole city?

This is a true difficulty, and the Church does not hide it. The Second Vatican Council says that the books of the Old Testament contain some things that are “incomplete and temporary” (Dei Verbum 15). Pope Benedict XVI says of such “dark” passages that revelation entered a history marked by the violence of its age, and that God’s people were led step by step toward the fullness of Christ (Verbum Domini 42). Many scholars add that the account is a later telling with a religious purpose. Whatever history lies behind it, the story is no pattern for how any people are to be treated. Jesus has shown us who God is: “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44).
study: God binds himself to remember. Which of his promises do I need to remember today?
Paul says “no condemnation”. Where am I still living as if I were under sentence?
What would it change if I really believed that those I have lost are alive to God?

lead: Today’s readings are about what a changed life looks like. The Letter to the Ephesians is practical: tell the truth, end your anger before sunset, work so that you can share, forgive. In Matthew, a father asks his two sons to work in the vineyard, and what counts is not the first answer but what they do in the end. Tax collectors and prostitutes who changed their minds are going in ahead. The Great Fast is the season of the second thought.

set: The letter’s second half turns from what God has done to how the baptized should live. Just before this, the writer has spoken of putting off the old self and clothing oneself with the new (4:22–24). Now he makes that concrete. The Church receives the letter as from Paul in prison; many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name, while others defend Paul’s authorship.
str: v. 25: truth, because we are one body.
vv. 26–27: anger must not last.
v. 28: from stealing to working and sharing.
vv. 29–30: words that build up; do not grieve the Spirit.
vv. 31–32: put away and put on: forgive as God forgave.
kw: The resentment that a provocation leaves behind, the anger that stays. This is the one that must not outlast the day.
“Do not make room for the devil.” Literally a place. Long-kept anger is like giving him a room in the house.
This verb is related to charis, grace. To forgive is to give a gift to someone who has no claim on it, as God has done to us.
vv: So then, putting away falsehood, let all of us speak the truth to our neighbors, for we are members of one another.
The first words echo Zechariah 8:16. The reason given is striking. Lying in the Church is like one part of the body deceiving another.
Be angry but do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger,

The first phrase comes from the Greek form of Psalm 4:4, which the Malayalam POC’s psalm also reflects. Anger as such is not called a sin, but it has a time limit. A simple rule for any home: do not go to sleep on it.
And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, with which you were marked with a seal for the day of redemption.
The verse sits among rules on speech. An unkind word causes pain to more than the one who hears it. In baptism and chrismation we were sealed, and the Spirit is a Person who can be grieved.
and be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you.
The word “as” gives both the model and the power. We forgive because we have been forgiven.
ch: The Catechism defines anger as a desire for revenge and warns against it (CCC 2302), and it speaks of the Spirit’s seal (CCC 698, 1274). When it comes to the petition “forgive us our trespasses”, it quotes this verse and says that such forgiveness is impossible by our own strength, and possible through the Spirit (CCC 2842).

set: Jesus is in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. The chief priests and the elders have asked by what authority he acts (21:23), and they will not answer his question about John’s baptism (21:25–27). This parable, the first of three, is addressed to them. “You” in this passage means those leaders, not the Jewish people, many of whom were themselves the ones who believed John.
str: vv. 28–30: the father and the two sons.
v. 31a: the question and their own answer.
vv. 31b–32: the application: John, the tax collectors and the prostitutes.
kw: Used of the son in v. 29 and of the leaders in v. 32, who “did not change” even after seeing. It is a word for second thoughts.
The present tense is worth noticing. The others are on their way in now. The door has not been shut on the leaders, and there is still time.
John came teaching what God asks. “Righteousness” is a favourite word of Matthew’s: doing God’s will (compare 3:15; 5:6).
vv: He answered, ‘I will not’; but later he changed his mind and went.

A note on the text: the ancient manuscripts tell this parable in more than one order. In the NRSV the first son refuses and then goes. In the Malayalam POC, following other manuscripts, the first agrees and does not go, and the second refuses and then goes, so the answer is “the second”. The teaching is the same: the one who did the work is the one who did the will of the father.
Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going into the kingdom of God ahead of you.

Tax collectors worked for the occupying power, and were known for extortion. These were people whom nobody would expect to go first. Jesus does not call their sin good: they are ahead because they “believed” and turned.
and even after you saw it, you did not change your minds and believe him.
The leaders have seen conversions before their eyes. Sometimes the sign God gives us is the changed life of someone we had written off.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the prayer of faith consists not only in saying “Lord, Lord” but in disposing the heart to do the Father’s will (CCC 2611). This is the point of the parable, and of Matthew 7:21. The change Jesus calls for is first of all interior, a turning of the whole life (CCC 1430–1431). The Catechism also notes how Jesus scandalized some by eating with tax collectors and sinners (CCC 588), because no one is outside God’s call.

qa: Does this mean that sin does not matter, as long as one turns back at the end?

No. The tax collectors and prostitutes go ahead because they have believed and changed their lives. The parable warns the person who says “I go” and does not go, and it encourages the one who said “no” for years. It would be presumption to plan a late conversion (CCC 2092); nobody knows how long the day is. But it is never too late to go to the vineyard today.
study: Is there any anger I have carried past many sunsets? What first step could end it?
To which request of God have I said “I go, sir”, and not gone?

lead: This Sunday’s four readings ask what we are building, and for whom. At Babel people build a tower to make a name for themselves, and they end in confusion. In Joshua one man’s hidden plunder leaves the whole camp unable to stand, until the truth is brought into the open. Paul tells us that we owe nothing to the flesh: the Spirit has made us children of God, who may call him “Abba”. And in Matthew tenants take over a vineyard that is not theirs, and throw out the son, whom God then makes the cornerstone. Each page shows the human wish to own what can only be received, and God’s answer. The key words are name, hidden, children and stone.

set: This is the last story of the opening chapters of Genesis. From the sin in the garden through Cain and the flood, each story shows sin spreading and God’s mercy continuing. The next chapter will begin something new with the call of Abram. Genesis 10 has already listed the nations “with their own language” (10:5), and it has repeated God’s word to “fill the earth” (9:1). This story tells the other side of it: why peoples cannot understand one another.

Shinar is Babylonia (compare Daniel 1:2). Its cities had great stepped temple towers of baked brick, since stone was scarce in the river plain. The author, from a land of stone, describes the method as a curiosity (v. 3). The people of Babylon took their city’s name to mean “gate of the god”. This story gives the name a very different sense.
str: vv. 1–2: one language; they settle in Shinar.
vv. 3–4: “Come, let us”: bricks, a city, a tower, a name.
v. 5: the turning point: the Lord comes down.
vv. 6–7: “Come, let us”: God’s answer.
vv. 8–9: scattering; the place is called Babel.
¶ The story is built like a mirror. What they planned in vv. 3–4 is overturned in vv. 6–9. Their fear was being scattered (v. 4), and that is what happens (v. 8).
kw: “Let us make a name for ourselves.” The next chapter answers it: God promises Abram to “make your name great” (12:2). A name can be seized or received.
“With its top in the heavens” is an ancient way of saying very high, but here it also suggests that human beings are reaching God’s own place.
The Hebrew plays on the sound of Babel. It plays also on “let us make bricks” (nilbᵉnâ), whose consonants turn around in “let us confuse” (nāblâ). The builders’ work is undone in their own sounds.
vv: Then they said, “Come, let us build ourselves a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves;
They do not mention God at all. Bricks and cities are not the problem: the problem is the wish to be secure and famous without him. It is also a refusal of the command to spread over the earth (9:1).
The Lord came down to see the city and the tower, which mortals had built.
Here is the writer’s quiet humour. The tower that reaches to heaven is so small that God has to come down to see it. “Mortals” in Hebrew is “the sons of Adam”, the sons of dust.
Come, let us go down, and confuse their language there,

God answers their “Come, let us” with his own. Scholars explain the plural as God speaking with his heavenly court, or as a form of solemn self-address. This is judgement, and also mercy: it limits what a united pride could do (see the question below).
Therefore it was called Babel, because there the Lord confused the language of all the earth;
Babylon, the proudest city the writer knew, is remembered as the city of confusion.
ch: The Catechism says that the division into many nations was meant “to limit the pride of fallen humanity”, which was united only in its perverse ambition to forge its own unity as at Babel (CCC 57). It calls the gathering of the Church God’s reaction to the chaos that sin provoked (CCC 761). At Pentecost the crowd says, “in our own languages we hear them speaking about God’s deeds of power” (Acts 2:11). The languages do not vanish: they are gathered. St Augustine says that if pride caused the diversity of tongues, Christ’s humility has gathered those tongues together (Tractates on John 6; in substance).

r.h: What is hidden in the tent
set: After the victory at Jericho (Joshua 6), Israel goes up against the small town of Ai and is put to flight (7:2–5). Joshua tears his clothes and lies on his face before the ark until evening, asking God why he has brought them over the Jordan (7:6–9). The reader already knows what Joshua does not: Achan of the tribe of Judah has taken some of the devoted things (7:1). Today’s reading is God’s reply.
str: v. 10: “Stand up!”
v. 11: the diagnosis: Israel has sinned.
v. 12: the result: they cannot stand; God will not be with them.
v. 13: the remedy: sanctify yourselves.
v. 14: the procedure: tribe, clan, household, person.
v. 15: the penalty.
¶ What follows (7:16–26) tells how Achan was found, and how he confessed that he had hidden his plunder in the ground inside his tent.
kw: What has been given over wholly to God, and so may not be used. To take it is a kind of theft from God. The word occurs again and again here.
Literally, to cross over. The verb that took Israel over the Jordan is now used for crossing over the covenant. The story of entry is shadowed at once.
A deed that breaks the very fabric of the community. The word is used for the gravest offences in Israel (see Judges 20:6).
vv: Stand up! Why have you fallen upon your face?
Joshua’s prayer is real, but God sends him to deal with the truth. Prayer is no replacement for honest action. Sometimes the answer to “Why, Lord?” is “Get up, and look in the camp.”
Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I imposed on them.
One man did it, and God says “Israel”. The Bible knows that we are bound together in both blessing and guilt.
Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow;
Before the people can go forward they must prepare themselves before God. The Great Fast is this “tomorrow”: a time to make ready for the Pasch.
And the one who is taken as having the devoted things shall be burned with fire,

This is severe, and the story that follows includes Achan’s family in the punishment (7:24–25). We read it as a page of a harsher age. Scripture itself moves further: “A child shall not suffer for the iniquity of a parent” (Ezekiel 18:20). Its lasting lesson is the seriousness of sin against the community, not the penalty.
ch: Joshua urges Achan, “make confession to him. Tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me” (7:19). What was punished by fire there is healed in the Church by mercy: “If we confess our sins, he who is faithful and just will forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). The Catechism teaches that sin is first an offence against God and that it also damages communion with the Church (CCC 1440). “Every sin harms this communion” (CCC 953). So no sin is purely private, and the sacrament of Reconciliation reconciles us with God and with the Church (CCC 1468–1469).

set: Paul has opened this chapter with “no condemnation” (8:1) and has said that the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus lives within us (8:11). Now he draws the conclusion. The Letter was written around AD 57 to a community in Rome that included both Jews and Gentiles. For that reason the word “adoption” would have spoken to both: Paul uses it for Israel as well (9:4).
str: vv. 12–13: two ways of living, and where they lead.
v. 14: led by the Spirit: children of God.
v. 15: not slavery and fear, but adoption and “Abba”.
v. 16: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit.
v. 17: heirs with Christ, if we suffer with him.
kw: We do owe something, but not to the flesh. Paul stops mid-sentence without saying to whom. The whole chapter says to whom.
Literally, being placed as a son. In Roman law an adopted son received the family’s name and full rights of inheritance. Christ is the Son by nature; we become children by grace.

An Aramaic word for father, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). The early Greek-speaking Churches kept it untranslated (see Galatians 4:6). It speaks of closeness and also of obedience, for in Gethsemane it is followed by “not what I want, but what you want”.
Paul likes words beginning with “with”: joint heirs, suffer with, glorified with. All that belongs to Christ is shared.
vv: for if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.
“By the Spirit” is the key. The Fast is no contest of will-power: it is the Spirit’s work in us, and we cooperate with him. See the question below.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God.
To be led is to walk behind someone. The mark of a child of God is that he allows himself to be led.
you have received a spirit of adoption. When we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Greek word for “cry” is strong, a loud call. Liturgical prayer may be in the background. Paul sets it against fear: a slave is afraid, a child calls out.
it is that very Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God,

Our hope as God’s children comes from the Spirit’s own witness within us, and not from our own feelings on a given day. It is hope, not a certainty that makes perseverance needless (compare CCC 2005).
and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ
The verse goes on: “if, in fact, we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.” The way of the heir goes through the Cross. This is why the Great Fast leads to the Pasch.
ch: The Catechism teaches that grace makes us adopted children of God (CCC 1996), and it cites this passage. Baptism begins this life (CCC 1265). When we say “Our Father” we adore the one who has caused us to be reborn by adopting us as his children (CCC 2782). The call to share Christ’s suffering is open to everyone (CCC 618). The Great Fast is among the Church’s special times of penance (CCC 1438).

set: Jesus is in the Temple, in the last days of his life. The chief priests and the elders have asked about his authority (21:23), and this parable is spoken directly to them. Afterward “the chief priests and the Pharisees” understand “that he was speaking about them” (21:45). Mark and Luke also tell the parable (Mark 12:1–12; Luke 20:9–19).

Jesus’ hearers knew the opening at once. It takes up Isaiah 5:1–7: “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel”. Isaiah’s fault lay in the vines, which gave wild grapes. In Jesus’ story the vineyard is good, and the fault lies with those in charge of it. Absentee owners and tenant farmers were a familiar part of life in the Galilee of that time, and tenants paid rent with part of the crop.
str: v. 33: the owner and all he does for the vineyard.
vv. 34–36: he sends slaves twice; they are beaten and killed.
vv. 37–39: last of all, the son.
vv. 40–41: “What will he do?” Their own answer.
v. 42: Scripture: Psalm 118:22–23.
vv. 43–44: the kingdom taken and given; the stone.
¶ The three parables here (two sons, tenants, wedding banquet) rise in force, from a question about obedience to a question about what has been done to God’s Son.
kw: Farmers who work land that is not their own. Everything turns on forgetting this.

The word runs through the passage (vv. 34, 41, 43; the NRSV sometimes says “produce”). It is what the owner has been asking for all along. In Matthew, fruit means a life that does God’s will (7:19–21).

Literally “head of the corner”: the key stone that holds a building together. The early Church often used this text of the risen Christ (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7). Some scholars also note that Hebrew has a wordplay between “son” (bēn) and “stone” (’eben).
The word in v. 43 means a people or nation. Here it speaks of those, from any origin, who bear fruit. See the question below.
vv: Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
The owner’s hope seems almost foolish, and this is the patience of God. The Catechism notes that Jesus here calls himself “the Son”, as distinct from the “servants” God had sent before (CCC 443).
So they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.
In Mark the son is killed and then thrown out (Mark 12:8). In Matthew and Luke he is thrown out first, perhaps to recall that Jesus “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;
The story of the son ends in death. Jesus does not stop there: he turns to the psalm, which says what God will do. Rejection is not the last word.
Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people that produces the fruits of the kingdom.

“You” here is the leaders who are questioning him (21:23, 45). The same warning is addressed to the Church, which may also stop bearing fruit. Matthew’s Gospel gives the same warning to Christians (7:21–23; 22:11–14).
The one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and it will crush anyone on whom it falls.
A note on the text: some ancient manuscripts do not have this verse, as the NRSV’s footnote points out. Most include it, and it is read here. No one can stay neutral about this stone.
ch: The Catechism uses this parable to speak of the Church as God’s vineyard, whose true vine is Christ (CCC 755), and of the Lord as the stone that the builders rejected, and which has become the cornerstone (CCC 756). St Irenaeus argues from it that one and the same God sent both the prophets and his Son (Against Heresies IV, 36; in substance). St John Chrysostom dwells on the owner’s care: he planted, fenced, built, and left nothing undone, and he sent servant after servant (Homilies on Matthew 68; in substance).

qa: Does this parable mean that God has rejected the Jewish people?

No. The parable is aimed at those leaders who were questioning Jesus, as Matthew says (21:45). Many scholars think that the sharp wording also reflects painful disputes of Matthew’s own time between his community and synagogue leaders. The Second Vatican Council says plainly that the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism repeats that the Jewish people as a whole cannot be held responsible for Jesus’ death (CCC 597), and that the gifts and call of God to them are irrevocable (CCC 839). The warning applies to us as well: we too work in a vineyard that is not our own.
Is God afraid of what people can do? Is the Babel story against progress?

God’s words in Genesis 11:6 are written with irony: the tower he had to come down to see is hardly a threat to him. The danger is to the human race, which, united in pride, can do terrible harm. The Bible is not against bricks or cities. The Church honours science and technology, and asks that they serve the human person and respect moral limits (CCC 2293–2294).
“Put to death the deeds of the body”: does Paul mean that the body is bad?

No. The body is good; God created it, and it will rise. Here “deeds of the body” means the habits of a self closed against God, such as Paul lists elsewhere. Fasting does not punish the body. It disciplines desire and opens the heart to prayer and to the poor (CCC 1434, 1438).
rite: On this Fourth Sunday the Great Fast (Sauma Ramba) is drawing toward its midpoint. The story of Babel touches us closely: the East Syriac liturgy we have inherited grew up in Mesopotamia, the land this story calls Shinar. In that same land the Spirit gathered a Church of prayer and mission. Today, our Holy Qurbana is offered in Malayalam, Syriac, English, Hindi and many other languages, wherever our people have gone, around one altar. Syriac, too, is a form of Aramaic, the language in which Jesus said “Abba”, so that word is not far from home. During this week we may search the tent, as Israel had to: a good confession is the honest way forward.
study: For whose name am I building: in my work, my home, my parish?
Is there anything “hidden in the tent” that is weakening my family or my community? What would it take to bring it to light?
Paul says the Spirit moves us to cry “Abba”. How does this change the way I pray, and what I do when I am afraid?
What fruit is the owner of the vineyard asking of me this Great Fast? In what ways do I act as if the vineyard were mine?
